entries.title: Maryland Powers Past Bucknell, 96-67
entries.summary: Maryland pulled away from Bucknell for a win Monday in the season opener for both teams.
entries.content:
COLLEGE PARK, Md. (AP) — Andre Mills had 22 points and 11 rebounds and Maryland pulled away from Bucknell for a 96-67 win Monday in the season opener for both teams.

Mills scored the first points of Maryland’s season with a 3-pointer and helped the Terrapins turn a tight first half into a 44-30 advantage by the break.

Bucknell took a 25-23 lead with 7:14 left in the half before Maryland closed on a 21-5 run. Robert Jennings II and Mills each hit 3-pointers during the surge, and Mills scored five points in the final 45 seconds.

Maryland continued to separate after halftime, using its size to dominate the glass 54-22, including a 28-6 advantage in offensive rebounds.

Kaden House added 14 points off the bench, Pharrel Payne had 13 points and six rebounds.

Aleksander Pachucki led Bucknell with 23 points and made 7 of 11 from 3-point range. Rocco Lamuno added 12 points.

entries.title: Wizards Win 103-94 Over Magic
entries.summary: The Wizards played without Alex Sarr, who had started their first six games at center.
entries.content:
ORLANDO, Fla. (AP) — Anthony Davis had 29 points and eight rebounds, AJ Dybantsa added 21 points in his third NBA game and the Washington Wizards beat the Orlando Magic 103-94 Monday night.

Kyshawn George added 22 points and Trae Young added 15 points and nine assists for the Wizards, who shot 53% overall in handing the Magic a fourth straight loss on their home court.

Franz Wagner led the Magic with 24 points. Desmond Bane added 20 and Jamal Cain and Tristan da Silva each scored 10 points.

Young scored 10 points in a 13-2 Washington run after Orlando had taken a nine-point lead early in the second quarter.

Young's layup completed an 8-0 outburst that left the Wizards with a 79-68 lead, the largest of the game, after three quarters.

Davis made 12 of 17 shots and had three steals.

The Magic shot (11 for 39) 28.2% from 3-point range after making four of their first five.

The Wizards played without Alex Sarr (knee), who had started their first six games at center.

Paolo Banchero (ankle) missed his fifth straight game and Jalen Suggs (knee) missed a fourth straight game for the Magic. Anthony Black, who played 33 minutes in Sunday’s loss to Boston, was held out as a precaution in the back-to-back set.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: The Race is On
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 3, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Election Day, plans for East Potomac and White’s walk out.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10. Exit polling confirms that most of us would vote for this atmospheric policy of sunshine, highs topping 70 and low humidity — by a landslide. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

It’s Election Day! 

Here are the basics: Polling places in D.C. are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., and if you find yourself in line when polls are closing, you’ll still be allowed to cast a ballot. You can also leave a mail ballot at any of the 55 ballot drop boxes around the city or head to a post office — though you need to confirm that the postmark on your ballot envelope has today’s date.

Will there be any election snafus? Initial fears over possible federal interference or intimidation in D.C.’s election seem to have quieted down, as federal agents and the National Guard have been instructed to avoid local polling places. According to D.C. officials, they have to stay at least 50 feet away from a polling place’s main entrance unless they are voting.

There aren’t likely to be any big surprises in local races, largely because of the outsize role that June’s Democratic primary plays in the city’s politics. Still, tonight is expected to mark the official election of Janeese Lewis George as D.C.’s next mayor, marking the end of Mayor Muriel Bowser’s 12 years in office and heralding a new progressive alternative.

Another big change will happen on Capitol Hill, where D.C. will have a new nonvoting delegate to Congress since Eleanor Holmes Norton — who served for three decades — decided not to run again. Robert White is likely to win the seat, though he’s facing a challenge from Republican Denise Rosado and Statehood Green Kymone Freeman.

Voters will also be choosing council members in wards 1, 3, 5 and 6, and two at-large seats. The introduction of ranked-choice voting has somewhat scrambled voting in the at-large races, where D.C. voters long had two votes to use. They still do now — kind of. The council chair will also be on the ballot, though incumbent Phil Mendelson is expected to cruise to victory and his 29th straight year in office.

D.C. is a predominantly Democratic city, but that hasn’t stopped local Republicans from competing in some of the races.

And then there’s the ducks, of course. D.C. voters will have a chance to weigh in on Initiative 86, which if passed would ban the production and sale of foie gras in the city.





DEEP DIVE

There’s plenty of angst and anger down at East Potomac Park ahead of Nov. 15, the deadline that President Donald Trump has repeatedly set for closing the popular locale to begin a renovation and expansion of the existing municipal golf course.

The biggest fears are that in creating what Trump has promised will be a “World Class Championship Golf Course,” he’ll wipe out other uses of the park, especially if Ohio Drive — which rings the island — is demolished to make way for the new 18-hole course.

That’s left runners, walkers, cyclists, bird-watchers, fishermen and families torn between two emotions: angry that Trump may soon close a favorite destination and mournful that their most recent visit could well be their last.

“I’m down here because I wanted to protest this attempted takeover. I’m so angry about it,” Maryland resident and cyclist Krista Riddley told The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle over the weekend. “I’ve got to do some laps because I don’t know when this is going to end.”

But some East Potomac Park users want to make sure that sadness over the possible closure doesn’t turn into acceptance that it’s inevitable.

“The goal right now is to make sure it doesn’t get shut down,” said Rebecca Miller, the executive director of the D.C. Preservation League, one of the plaintiffs in ongoing litigation over Trump’s ever-evolving plans for the island.

To that end, her attorneys are planning to ask for a temporary restraining order this week in hopes of keeping public access to East Potomac Park while the legal battle plays out.





FROM THE DISTRICT

White officially resigned his seat on the D.C. Council yesterday to preserve his eligibility for the District’s congressional delegate race, capping a 10-year tenure on the council.

While White maintains a preelection resignation wasn’t legally required, he stepped down to avoid a “prolonged controversy.”

“I want to make sure that there is nothing that stands between, or even appears to stand between, this day and the next mission, which is on Capitol Hill,” White told supporters outside the Wilson Building.

The Kennedy Center’s financial crisis is becoming harder to separate from its planned closure. New court documents show that board Vice Chair Jennifer Fischer told Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick the institution was broke and borrowing money to pay its bills — even as the Trump administration argues a two-year shutdown is necessary to address the building’s deteriorating condition, The Sun’s Torrie Herrington reports.

And on Monday, Torrie reports, the center announced its 2026 honorees: Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell. For the first time, the award ceremony will not be hosted at the center but at Capital One Arena.

Officials foggy on power outage cause: A power outage in Foggy Bottom on Monday morning affected roughly 1,100 customers, including buildings used by the World Bank Group, State Department and George Washington University, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.

A Pepco spokesperson told The Sun in a statement that the cause was under investigation and there were no indications of foul play.

Midterms got you reaching for a drink? The Sun has rounded up where to get a buzz while watching results roll in.

Too close for comfort: Assuming that taxpayer dollars paid for it, Illinois’ Sen. Tammy Duckworth penned a letter Monday to several federal agencies criticizing Friday’s unexpected flyover as dangerously close to the ground and wasteful, The Washington Post reports.

Critical condition: Last month, Bowser asked the D.C. Council to support Cedar Hill Regional Medical Center, the taxpayer-funded hospital that opened last year in Ward 8, with $10 million a year for the next six years. Now, the Washington Business Journal reports that the struggling hospital has been hemorrhaging that figure — $10 million — each month for the past several quarters.





FROM VIRGINIA

Locked in: After the last Orange Line train carrying game attendees from Northwest Stadium entered Vienna station early Monday morning, some Commanders fans left their railcars to find themselves stuck behind locked gates, The Sun’s Justice and Will Hofmann report.





WHAT YOU GET NEAR METRO

This week’s real estate column looks at what buyers can get for under $1 million near a metro station in the D.C. area.

Where is this house listed? Click on your guess to see the answer:

  1. Maryland
  2. Virginia
  3. D.C.




SPORTS

The Maryland women’s basketball team nearly opened its season with a spectacular comeback, fighting back from a 31-point deficit against top-ranked South Carolina in an eventual 101-93 loss Monday. The game was played in Paris as part of the Oui-Play Paris games, writes The Sun’s Alex Schiffer.

Former Washington Post columnist and longtime “Pardon the Interruption” co-host Michael Wilbon announced an indefinite leave of absence from his ESPN duties Monday. Wilbon, who will turn 68 this month, cited “multiple health issues”in a post on X. “The goal is to come out of it feeling much better than I do now and ready to return to sparring with [Tony Kornheiser].”

What to Watch Today:

NHL: Capitals vs. Dallas, 7 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was C) The Octagon. A special shoutout to Bob Witeck, who answered first.

The newsletter was produced by Greta Forslund, Gaby Morera Di Núbila and Jaden Amos.

entries.title: Ballot Scanners Fail Across New York’s Westchester County
entries.summary: Until the issue is resolved, election workers will have to count votes by hand.
entries.content:
The New York Attorney General’s Office said it is monitoring a widespread technical issue with ballot scanning machines in Westchester County that may force the county’s election workers to count votes by hand.

None of the county’s voting machines were operating on Tuesday morning, authorities said. It is unclear when they will be back online, though New York Attorney General Letitia James said county officials are working to resolve the issue.

“Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations. Your votes will count,” James said on X.

Westchester County is one of the most populous counties in the state and sits just outside of New York City. Polls show the race between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, who is running for reelection in the district that encompasses much of the county, and Democratic candidate Cait Conley is a toss-up.

In a statement posted to X, the Westchester County Board of Elections said it is communicating with state and local officials and poll workers to address the issue.

Voters are being encouraged to remain in line and vote. Their ballots will be placed in orange emergency ballot bags that will remain secure and monitored, the board said.

Officials will then count the votes in accordance with applicable election procedures.

“Let us be absolutely clear: Every eligible vote will be counted,” the board said, apologizing for the inconvenience posed by the issue.

“No voter should be discouraged from participating in this election because of this issue. Your voice matters. Your vote matters. Please stay in line and vote.”

Lawler also confirmed an issue with the ballot scanners and encouraged voters to stay in line.

“We do not yet know the exact cause of the issue, whether it is the ballot or the machine,” Lawler said. “The Board of Elections is working with their vendors to resolve it.”

Some Republicans almost immediately suggested that the malfunction was part of a coordinated attack by Democrats to rig the midterm elections, an insinuation that follows President Donald Trump’s debunked claims of widespread voter fraud across the country.

“No surprise. The Democrats in NY will do anything and everything to cheat,” Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-New York), who serves as chair of the House Election Integrity Caucus, wrote on X.

Conservative commentator Laura Loomer, a Trump confidante, echoed Tenney’s remarks.

“Democrats are already trying to steal the election in New York today,” she wrote. “What are the odds the ballot machines in Westchester County aren’t working?”

She added: “Democrats only know how to cheat.”

entries.title: Man Charged With Mailing Letters Containing Powder to Officials Ahead of the Election
entries.summary: Federal authorities said the man sent hundreds of letters containing nonhazardous white powder.
entries.content:
OKLAHOMA CITY — Federal authorities have charged an Oklahoma man with sending hundreds of letters containing nonhazardous white powder to public officials ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.

The powders turned out to be yeast or flour, though not all letters have been fully tested, the FBI said in a court filing made public Tuesday.

Robin Martin is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. Martin was expected to make his initial court appearance Tuesday afternoon in Oklahoma City. Online records do not list an attorney to comment on his behalf.

Federal authorities announced last month that they were investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that had been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and urged recipients to treat the mailings as “potentially hazardous.”

A message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms obtained by The Associated Press said that law enforcement officials were working to intercept any additional letters, but “it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations.”

The FBI said at the time that the bureau and the Postal Inspection Service were investigating. The FBI referred questions to the U.S. attorney’s office Tuesday, and the Postal Inspection Service didn’t immediately return an email message from the AP seeking comment.

entries.title: East Potomac Golf Course Plans Outline Tiered Pricing, Seawall Rehabilitation
entries.summary: The plans include the projected cost of a new seawall, a safety assessment of the facilities and plans for displaced recreational areas.
entries.content:
The Interior Department submitted plans for its massive redevelopment of East Potomac Golf Links, detailing the cost and timeline for a new seawall and a tiered-pricing concept but leaving the total cost and timeline of the project unclear.

The plans, sent to the National Capital Planning Commission on Friday, come as President Donald Trump’s plans for a “world class championship” golf course move through an ongoing legal battle ahead of a planned closure date of Nov. 15. The commission will consider the plans at a meeting on Dec. 3.

The plans describe the golf course as “dilapidated” and “unsafe,” and outline a goal of transforming it into an “affordable championship golf course, open to the public.”

The 55-page proposal includes safety assessments that mark nearly every aspect of the golf course as being in poor condition. One assessment found the clubhouse interior, driving range and trees in the parking lot to be in “critical” condition, and 84 fire and life safety deficiencies were flagged around the facility.

A focal point of the proposal is the rehabilitation of the aging seawall surrounding the man-made island with a “cost-effective” model.

The work would include installing about 20,700 feet of new seawall made with a combination of stamped concrete and stacked stone. The proposal estimates the new seawall would cost $304.5 million — $56 million less than an all-stone version — and would take two-and-a-half to three-and-a-half years to complete.

The cost estimate comes after a hearing on Friday in which U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes castigated the Department of Justice for not being able to precisely say where the funding for the project would come from. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said at the hearing that the new seawall would cost between $150 million and $400 million, according to three estimates, and that government funds are available for such projects.

The proposal outlined how the redevelopment would address the displaced recreational areas surrounding the current golf course — an issue that has been a source of anxiety for many park users as Trump’s plans have developed.

The new 18-hole “championship”-style golf course would extend to the shoreline, covering the pedestrian walkways that bikers and joggers often use. The redevelopment is also expected to remove picnic and fishing areas around Hains Point.

The Interior Department plans to “locate replacements” for recreation areas “as close as feasible, such as West Potomac Park and the Tidal Basin.”

The proposal bases the redeveloped golf course's projected economic impact on the reported success of three other public golf courses across the country: Memorial Park in Houston; Bethpage Black in Long Island, New York; and Torrey Pines in San Diego.

It pitches a two-tier pricing model, where D.C. residents would pay a lower rate — similar to the three cited golf courses, which charge two to four times more for nonresidents to play. The plan says that nonresidents paying a higher price would help fund the new course’s upkeep.

“Premium out-of-town fees support championship conditions while locals keep affordable access,” the proposal says.

Currently, East Potomac Golf Links doesn’t offer different rates for residents, and its website lists the most expensive round of golf as $48 for 18 holes on the Blue course on weekends.

entries.title: Ruben Gallego Tests His Blueprint Ahead of 2028: Latinos and Young Men
entries.summary: At stops in El Paso and Miami, the Arizona senator tried to build name recognition and test the appetite for his politics outside his home state.
entries.content:
EL PASO, Texas — Before he took the stage, most people in the rally crowd had no idea who he was, and the few who could remember ever hearing his name could recall only vague biographical facts: Didn’t he serve in the military? Wasn’t he raised by his mom?

He was short. They knew that now, because the governor of New Mexico had just made a joke about it. They learned he was a champion for the Democratic Party, a fighter who had beaten a Republican in a red state, a model for the upset they were all here rooting for.

“Help me welcome Senator Gallego!” the governor said.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, took the microphone. He riffed on the governor’s joke about his height, which got a laugh, and launched into a boilerplate rally speech for a couple hundred people at the Epic Railyard Event Center.

He was here in late October, on a five-stop swing through heavily Latino midterm battlegrounds in Nevada, Texas and Florida, to test the appetite for his politics outside his home state before potentially running for president.

Among political insiders, Gallego’s rising star has dulled in recent months. He was close friends with former Rep. Eric Swalwell of California, who is under federal investigation for sexual misconduct, and Gallego has faced questions about what he knew. Gallego himself was also accused by one House member of campaign finance violations and sexual misconduct; the Senate Ethics committee dismissed the complaint in June.

But Gallego, 46, has reportedly eyed his party’s presidential nomination since shortly after he won his seat in 2024. He’s made trips to Iowa, New Hampshire and South Carolina. And like other potential candidates, he has spent recent months courting possible donors.

Days before the midterm elections, though, he was still deflecting questions about running.

“I can't have a long race,” he told me. “I just don't think I could be a good father and a good candidate at the same time, and so we’re going to decide what’s best for my family.”

When Democratic strategist Jesse Lehrich looked at the potential primary field, he saw hope for the senator, writing in an email: “A lot of these guys are talented, but they have no differentiation and no narrative; Gallego has both of those things.”

JKG00387.jpg (3563x2380, AR: 1.50)
Gallego grew up poor. He had an abusive father who left the family. He went to Harvard, where he served drinks at parties held by Pete Buttigieg, and he fought in Iraq, where his best friend was killed. He scaled the political ladder, from the Phoenix City Council to the Senate, and he became one of his party’s best communicators with Latinos and young men — two key groups in the Democrats’ quest to take back the White House.

“Will it be enough to catapult him to the upper echelon of 2028 contenders?” Lehrich wrote. “Hard to say; certainly not overnight. … But I do think he has a lot more upside, and a more realistic path, than many presidential hopefuls.”

During his travels, Gallego said, he’s realized Latino men are angrier and more fearful now than they were in 2022 or 2024. The men feel an existential responsibility to protect and provide for their families, he said, and they’re struggling to do so because of the rising cost of living and the overreach of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The senator, who is known for channeling his anger in frank, often profane speech, acknowledged this moment might feel more natural to him than to other politicians.

Could the blueprint that worked in Arizona in 2024 work in Las Vegas and San Antonio, suburbs and small towns, all across the Sun Belt and all across the nation?

“Wherever I've gone with that message, it has resonated very strongly,” Gallego said. “And some people, by time I get there, already have heard my message. That tells me that people are interested.”

* * *

One of Gallego’s biggest problems flared up at the dawn of the tour.

Early last Monday morning, as he prepped for a day of events in Las Vegas, FBI agents raided a mansion in Beverly Hills as part of the agency’s investigation into Swalwell.

Swalwell, who was accused by five women of sexual assault and harrassment, has denied and vowed to fight the allegations. Gallego has said that, while he knew his longtime close friend was “flirty,” he “never saw him engage in any of the predatory behavior.”

Gallego declined to comment on whether he’d ever visited the mansion, as well as on the progress of the investigation.

The mansion is owned by timeshare billionaire Stephen Cloobeck, who let Swalwell live there for a time, and who, according to campaign finance records, donated to Gallego’s senate campaign the maximum allowable amount of $3,300.

When asked about his relationship with Cloobeck, Gallego said, “He was just a donor. He donated to many other campaigns.”

Later that day, in Vegas, Gallego met with a major hospitality workers’ union (also one of the largest immigrant organizations in the early-primary state) and campaigned with the Democratic candidate for governor, Aaron Ford, at a market called El Mercado.

Gallego, pundits say, is an ideal surrogate in Latino communities. Last year, he attended rallies for the eventual governors of Virginia and New Jersey, and he stumped for the eventual first female and first non-Hispanic mayor of Miami. This year, Tejano musician Bobby Pulido, who is running in a Texas district that President Donald Trump won by 18 points in 2024, told Semafor that he didn’t want visits from national Democrats — except Gallego, whom he called a “friend of mine.”

AP88368032216.jpg (4199x2882, AR: 1.46)
U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)The next day, in Nevada’s deep red 2nd Congressional District, Gallego championed Democratic nominee Teresa Benitez-Thompson. He seemed to disdain her Republican opponent, David Flippo, who is embroiled in a stolen-valor controversy.

“David Flippo has zero character,” Gallego said in a video, an edge in his voice. “As an Iraq war veteran myself, I can’t imagine someone like him being able to go to this office after lying about his Bronze Star citation. He knew he was lying. He kept that lie up.”

In Texas, Gallego started in San Antonio, where he campaigned for Democratic nominee Katy Padilla Stout in the historically red 23rd District, and then he flew to El Paso to campaign for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa.

In the industrial-chic wedding venue, only one of the two dozen rally goers interviewed for this article knew Gallego. Yvonne Gomez, a 64-year-old retiree, was aware of his military service and election integrity efforts. (In June, Gallego co-sponsored a bill to prevent Trump from using military or federal law enforcement to interfere with the midterm elections.) But like all Democrats, she said, Gallego needed to do more than oppose Trump to get her vote.

“I want a plan,” she explained. “I don’t care about retribution. … We’ve got bigger issues.”

Billy Estrada, a 21-year-old political science student at the University of Texas-El Paso, said he didn’t know who Gallego was and that he shouldn’t run for president. He preferred Democrats to nominate Kamala Harris, California Gov. Gavin Newsom or New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

“You should select someone to represent your party that’s well-known,” he said. “If you’re going to go against a mascot name [like Trump], [your candidate] should be a mascot name, too.”

After Gallego began speaking, the people who had chairs, who were on their third speech of the night, all sat down. And as he spoke, the crowd was enthusiastic but not raucous. They booed mentions of Trump, Elon Musk and Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. They cheered his version of the party’s messages on corruption and affordability. And when Gallego mentioned the pain of taking trucks to the gas pump, a man in the back said, “Yep!”

Gallego never mentioned the finer points of the sweeping economic agenda he unveiled last month. But he mentioned again and again part of its title: “the American Dream.” In 2024, he significantly outperformed Harris by winning groups that otherwise embraced Trump, such as Latinos, young men and the working class, especially those without college degrees. A big part of his success, he has said, was talking about restoring the American Dream.

Research from a Democratic nonprofit called Winning Jobs NarrEliott Rodriguez, the Democratic candidate for Florida’s 27th District, welcomes Gallego on his tour bus just south of Miami last Thursday. Jayme Kaye Gershen for The Washington Sunbroative consistently finds voters don’t just want prices to come down, according to Executive Director Steve Pierce. People want to build good lives by doing things like buying a home, saving some money for retirement and enjoying a few luxuries, such as the “big-ass trucks” Gallego talks about.

JKG00558.jpg (3615x2410, AR: 1.50)
“Democrats have spent a lot of time talking about the struggles people face, and that may serve them well in this election,” Pierce wrote in an email. “But the long-term opportunity for people like Gallego who may have aspirations to lead the party forward is to articulate a compelling vision for what a better economic future could look like and how we get there.”

Near the end of the speech, Gallego got personal. When he was a kid, he said, he spent “many years” in Chihuahua, the Mexican state just over the border, and he often came back to the U.S. through their city.

“I remember many times crossing the border with my family. It always had this special meaning to me, that I was in a safe space, that I had a future. And the last time that I crossed the border, to move permanently back to the States, I remember seeing it with my primos, looking out at the desert sky, seeing what an amazing place this was.

“My first version of America was always El Paso.”

Not everyone was moved. An older man accused Gallego of pandering, and others who liked the story still couldn’t remember his name. Andres Berrios, a 19-year-old mariachi, said he missed the moment because he got up in the middle of the speech to get a Dr Pepper.

But several people who’d never heard of him an hour ago found it endearing.

“It was heartfelt,” said Angela Camacho, a 34-year-old teacher.

“He got me,” said Corina Martinez, 39, holding her fist to her heart.

* * *

On a tour bus south of Miami, Gallego sat across from Democratic candidate Eliott Rodriguez.

Rodriguez, a former TV journalist, was in a tough battle for Florida’s 27th Congressional District. His Republican opponent, Rep. María Elvira Salazar, had money and history on her side; the district had only elected one Democrat since 2012. But Cook Political Report had declared the race “clearly competitive.”

"What's been the biggest surprise?" Gallego asked the first-time candidate.

“Dealing with different personalities on the campaign," Rodriguez said. “But I’ve been able to manage that.”

And then Rodriguez started telling Gallego his family’s immigration story, which ran through Cuba, rather than El Paso, but hit similar notes.

As Gallego listened, it was easy to see how he developed rapport with downballot candidates and the power brokers around them.

JKG00179.jpg (4026x2689, AR: 1.50)JKG00928 copy.jpg (4156x2776, AR: 1.50)The groundwork did not always translate to attention on the internet. Local media coverage of Gallego’s tour was thin outside of El Paso, and when his PR team posted a handful of highlight reels and influencer-coded videos on social media, nearly all hit modest, four-figure view counts. A few early X posts were overwhelmed by users linking him to Swalwell. The most engagement Gallego got on the tour was on unrelated posts criticizing Trump and Republicans.

Any Democratic candidate for president, Gallego believes, would need to win at least 62% of the Latino vote. In 2024, Kamala Harris got 56%, down 10 percentage points from Joe Biden in 2020. Among Latino men, Trump pulled off a stunning 35-point swing.

After the midterms, Gallego said, he would measure the success of his trip by numbers. Did his candidates win? Did they turn out more Latinos than expected? Or, more specifically, did they get a higher share of the votes from Latino men?

“That's the area that I think really matters,” he said, “to basically prove a lot of our thesis, which is: You can get these voters back, but you have to kind of focus on the things that actually matter to them.”

Standing in a parking lot outside a polling place in Miami, admiring Rodriguez’s catchy campaign song, Gallego insisted the mission was bigger than his potential bid for the White House.

“We can't win nationally without Latinos,” he said. “There's just no other way. The math doesn't math. It's our responsibility [to reach them], because we want to make sure the country does well. ... We have to help, whether I'm running or not."

entries.title: Local Officials Are Keeping the DOJ’s Election Monitors 100 Feet Away
entries.summary: The department told The Washington Sun that it will comply with any state laws that require monitors to stand back from the entrance to polling sites.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is sending Department of Justice election monitors to all 50 states for the first time, but they won't be allowed to enter polling sites in several cities and counties.

Virginia’s Prince William County, Arkansas’ Pulaski County and Minnesota’s Hennepin and Ramsey counties — home to the state’s “Twin Cities” of Minneapolis and St. Paul — are among the jurisdictions that have denied the department’s request for access ahead of Election Day, saying that state law requires them to remain a certain distance away from the entrance to polling sites.

“Federal monitors may be at polling places in Hennepin County but they may not be IN the polling place,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty wrote in a statement Monday. “They need to be 100 feet away just like any other member of the public who is not there to vote.”

Hennepin and Ramsey counties also denied the Justice Department’s observers access to polling sites during the state’s primary elections in August.

Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon plans to examine the DOJ’s election teams and “monitor the monitors,” but he told CBS News the federal observers who came to the state during the primary had “abided by all applicable laws and rules.”

Laws in a number of states, including Minnesota, Colorado and Arkansas, require unauthorized individuals, including federal observers, to remain 100 feet away from polling locations. Virginia’s statutes require only a 40-foot buffer zone.

The department said it plans to comply with all state rules that deny monitors from directly accessing polling sites, DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told The Washington Sun.

“State or local approval is not required for Department monitoring,” Pels said. “However, Department monitors follow the state and local laws and rules that govern polling locations, and every monitor is trained on the rules for their assigned jurisdiction.”

“So no, they will not enter polling sites in violation of a state law,” she added. “They will remain at a distance, as required.”

The DOJ has sent election monitors to polling locations in past election cycles, but the poll-watching efforts under President Donald Trump have ramped up this year. The department plans to deploy 1,000 monitors across the country Tuesday, with Harmeet K. Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, describing the push as the “largest monitoring effort in DOJ history.”

Upon denying access, county officials typically cite state laws that will require the DOJ’s election monitors to stay a certain distance away from polling sites.

“Unauthorized individuals, including federal monitors, must keep a distance of 100 feet from the building in which a polling place is located,” Ramsey County wrote on its website.

Prince William County Registrar Eric Olsen told the DOJ in an email denying their request for access that he “cannot be confident the observers sent will have the training, temperament, and expertise to meet this artificial goal,” the Prince William Times reported Thursday.

Democrats have been sounding the alarm about the DOJ’s monitors ahead of Election Day. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Alex Padilla (D-California) announced earlier this month that more than 100 trained Senate Democratic staff members would be deployed across nine states as “official congressional election observers.”

“Donald Trump has made clear that he wants to ‘take over the voting’ in state-run elections. Election interference is unconstitutional and illegal and Congress will be watching,” Padilla said.

entries.title: Trump Says U.S. Will Halt $4 Billion in Aid to Israel
entries.summary: The president said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea.
entries.content:
By Ben Finley, Matthew Lee and Darlene Superville

WASHINGTON — The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East, President Donald Trump said on Tuesday.

The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Election Day for the midterms that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years.

Trump said Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel.

“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”

There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu’s office.

Tens of Billions of Dollars Have Gone to Israel

The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the last few years.

In 2016, President Barack Obama, a Democrat, signed an unprecedented security agreement with Israel to give its military $38 billion over 10 years, amounting to $3.8 billion a year. Under the agreement, Israel’s ability to spend part of the funds on Israeli military products was to be phased out and eventually all of the money would be spent on American military industries.

Netanyahu has talked about the need to wean Israel off the aid in the past and has said that the American aid would end at some point.

He told The Economist in January that he wanted to “taper off” U.S. military aid in the next 10 years and that such a change was “in the works.”

Trump Says Critics Can Easily Target the $4 Billion Payment

But the optics of the aid had also become an issue, according to Trump, who singled out El-Sayed for using it as a talking point.

“The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” Trump said Tuesday on Fox. “And we can’t allow that to happen. I don’t like that, because it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target. And Bibi and I have been talking, and we’ve agreed. He was very understanding of it.”

Phasing out direct military and economic aid to Israel has long been a subject of debate in both countries and has gained traction in the last several years.

There are several issues that complicate it, though, not least of which are obligations the U.S. has to Israel under the terms of the Camp David peace accords with Egypt, which require the United States to support Israel and Egypt with security assistance.

In addition, much of the assistance the U.S. provides Israel comes in the form of foreign military financing, or FMF, that gives Israel the money but requires it to spend the money on American-produced weaponry, meaning the funds are plowed back into the U.S. economy.

Unless Israel plans to spend the same amount on purchasing American materiel, U.S. defense contractors may see an impact.

There Was More Aid After the Gaza War Started

An academic study published last year showed the U.S. under the administrations of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and Trump provided at least $21.7 billion in military assistance to Israel after the start of the Gaza war in 2023. The study was published on the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel that provoked the conflict.

Another study, also published last year by the Costs of War project at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs, said the U.S. had spent roughly $10 billion more on security aid and operations in the broader Middle East in the previous two years.

While the reports relied on open source material for most of their findings, they offered some of the most comprehensive accountings of U.S. military aid to close ally Israel and estimated costs of direct American military involvement in the Middle East.

entries.title: Federal Judge Allows DOJ Poll Monitors From Law Enforcement Agencies
entries.summary: The Justice Department was instructed to ensure the poll monitors would be administrative workers and not sworn federal agents.
entries.content:
A federal judge declined Monday night to prohibit the Justice Department from sending employees from federal law enforcement agencies to monitor polling places.

U.S. District Judge Reggie Walton pressed the department during a Monday hearing for more information about why it decided to deploy hundreds more poll monitors and enroll for the first time in that effort workers from the Bureau of Prisons, Drug Enforcement Administration and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. But he ultimately decided that at this stage the presence of employees from those agencies does not intimidate voters.

“The evidence indicates that the personnel that will work as election monitors will not be armed with firearms, not be in uniform, not carry any insignia of their law enforcement association, and will not be sworn law enforcement officials and therefore will not possess the power to arrest,” Walton, a George W. Bush appointee, wrote in his eleventh-hour ruling.

Although the Justice Department has stated that it would have 1,000 poll monitors across the country, it unveiled the specific locations in all states Tuesday morning. The government has clarified in court filings that FBI and Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees will not be at the polls.

The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division took reasonable steps to ensure sworn law enforcement officers wouldn’t be part of the detail monitoring the polls, according to court filings the federal government submitted Monday night and Tuesday morning.

“It is inconceivable that anything could happen at a polling place where a BOP employee serving in a monitoring capacity would be authorized to make an arrest,” a filing from the Justice Department states.

Walton ordered that the Justice Department act to ensure the poll monitors would indeed be administrative workers.

The NAACP sued to block the Justice Department from having any personnel monitoring the polls who work in federal law enforcement agencies. The lawsuit is one of the several legal battles developing ahead of the hotly contested midterm elections.

Despite the court’s refusal to grant the emergency block NAACP sought, the civil rights organization said it views the outcome as a victory. 

“We mounted this litigation because voter intimidation remains a problem today and federal law enforcement has no place in our polling sites,” Kristen Clarke, the general counsel for the NAACP, said in a press release. “Through this litigation we have limited DOJ’s poll monitoring activities and our polling places will be absolutely free of federal law enforcement on Election Day."

Walton also sought reassurances that the department didn’t pick the poll monitor locations based on perceived political leanings of those areas.

“I would hope that within our country that would not be the norm,” Walton said during the hearing, emphasizing that he expected the locations to have been picked randomly.

The department chose where to send the monitors based on the locations of U.S. Attorney Offices and historical practices, including where language access is an issue, according to a Monday evening declaration from Eric Neff, the acting chief of the Civil Rights Division’s Voting Section.

Walton expressed frustration with what he said appeared to be conflicting statements from Justice Department attorney Kathryn Barragan.

Barragan said that the employees from the law enforcement agencies were clerical workers and didn’t have authority to carry out arrests. A declaration the federal government submitted states that the department’s Civil Rights Division does not track the title of the employees who volunteer, but that it has taken appropriate steps to avoid engaging any sworn law enforcement agents.

After a back-and-forth, the judge said that if the federal government had given a false representation of its plans, “somebody is going to pay a price for that.”

entries.title: Corporations Are Capitalizing on the ‘Citizens United’ Decision Like Never Before
entries.summary: In 2026, direct political spending from companies’ treasuries hit historic highs.
entries.content:
Direct corporate political spending reached new heights during the 2026 midterms, with hundreds of millions of dollars flowing into federal-level campaigns, according to government campaign finance data.

This spending represents an evolution in American elections in the years following the Supreme Court’s 2010 decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which in part allowed companies to use money from their corporate treasuries to advocate for or against political candidates.

Geosor Corp. — liberal billionaire George Soros’ investment firm — blockchain company Ripple and industrial conglomerate Koch Inc. lead all corporations in direct political spending, according to federal data compiled by nonpartisan research organization OpenSecrets.

Two cryptocurrency giants — Crypto.com’s parent company and Coinbase — as well as two gambling sportsbooks — DraftKings and FanDuel — also rank among the nation’s largest corporate political spenders, according to OpenSecrets.
Bitcoin.crypto (5616x3744, AR: 1.50)Tobacco company Altria, private prison and reentry company GEO Group and oil companies Chevron and Occidental Petroleum have also each spent millions of dollars on federal-level politics so far this election cycle.

The corporations, which have significant legal, regulatory and sometimes government contracting business with the federal government, have donated most of this money to various super PACs, which may raise and spend unlimited amounts to promote or attack political candidates.

The most popular recipient of direct corporate contributions this election cycle: President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC.

Until recently, most corporations avoided making direct political contributions for fear of reputational injury and customer blowback.

Instead, they’d often prefer to make indirect contributions through politically active “dark money” nonprofits or stick strictly to making contributions funded by corporate executives through traditional political action committees, which are limited to $5,000 per candidate per election, and $15,000 to national party committees per year.

OpenSecrets has tracked $654 million in direct corporate donations this cycle, while a newly released report from progressive think tank Public Citizen pegs the total at $737 million — a 60% increase from an already record-breaking 2024 cycle.

“Following the Citizens United ruling, corporations mostly held back from exploiting their new ability to spend unlimited sums on elections,” Public Citizen wrote in its report. “The norm against direct engagement by Big Business is eroding.”

After cryptocurrency — which makes up just over a fifth of all corporate spending this cycle — the “casino, racetracks & gambling” and “private equity & investment firms” industries directly spent the most on federal elections this cycle, according to OpenSecrets.
FanDuel (4925x3277, AR: 1.50)Corporations spent money to support conservative interests at four times the rate of liberal ones, OpenSecrets found. Corporate donors gave over $370 million to conservative interests alone, according to the organization.

This doesn’t count corporate “dark money,” which remains a major force in politics. This means what’s readily known about corporate political spending is “most definitely an undercount,” said Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist for Public Citizen.

Few of the corporations The Washington Sun reached out to for an interview regarding their political spending responded, and Ripple declined to comment.

Circle — a major cryptocurrency and financial technology company — and its subsidiary donated more than $4 million this cycle. However, it didn’t just support one party, instead donating $500,000 to the Democrats’ Senate Majority PAC and the same amount to Republicans’ Senate Leadership Fund.

“Circle supports candidates from both parties who want clear digital asset rules that protect consumers, advance American innovation, and reinforce the U.S. dollar’s global role,” the company told The Sun in a statement.

OpenSecrets tracked over $8.8 million in contributions from Pivotal Ventures this cycle, some of which went to Democratic-supporting organizations Women Vote!, Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy PAC and Womencount PAC.

Pivotal Ventures is a private investment firm founded by billionaire Melinda French Gates that focuses on women's issues across the globe. A spokesperson for the firm emphasized to The Sun that the company's political investments reflect the organization's mission.
Melinda.French.Gates (2400x3216, AR: 0.75)Components of health insurance giant UnitedHealth Group donated $5 million to MAGA Inc. early last year, according to FEC data. UnitedHealth Group gave less than $27,000 to liberal recipients, according to OpenSecrets’ analysis.

Like Circle, Anthony Marusic, a spokesperson for UnitedHealth, told The Sun in an email that the company has “a long history of bipartisan policy engagement, and we support elected officials who share our commitment to making healthcare more affordable and accessible.”

Fairshake, a super PAC fueled by the cryptocurrency industry, helped supercharge the trend toward direct political spending in elections, said Brendan Glavin, the director of insights at OpenSecrets. Corporations are increasingly inclined to decide, “We’re going to pick the candidates that we like and we’re going to spend heavily in their races,’” Glavin said.

But why is this happening now? Crypto and AI, relatively new industries, have lots of cash to work with, while at the same time “there’s a lot of money at stake with the regulatory issues,” Glavin said.

“Everything’s moving very fast in AI, and there’s a lot of questions about regulation,” he said. “And crypto, they’re trying to get legislation through that is favorable to them, and that’s been held up.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Volleyball Players of Week 10
entries.summary: This week’s standouts include high-flying outside hitters from CMIT North and National Cathedral.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

With the volleyball regular season in the books, it’s officially playoff time in the DMV. Here are three players who got the job done to earn All-DMV volleyball player of the week:

A’vielle Lewis, Sophomore, Outside Hitter, CMIT North

Last week’s Prince George’s County championship game provided a raucous atmosphere for a battle between two of the county’s most dominant volleyball programs: CMIT North and Eleanor Roosevelt. Lewis, the Golden Tigers’ dominant outside hitter, said it was the loudest gymnasium she’s played in this fall.

Despite all the noise, Lewis met the moment and helped her team make some school history. The sophomore outside hitter racked up 32 kills in a 3-1 victory over the Raiders, giving coach Mark Snyder’s team its first-ever county championship victory.

The Golden Tigers leaned on her early and often — Lewis provided a barrage of kills in the first set to give her team an early advantage. After dropping the second set, Snyder’s team turned to Lewis time and again.

“I really feel like from the beginning of the season we were really working hard during the summer, so I knew that we were going to get far,” Lewis said after the victory. “I feel like we have a good chance of winning states, so I’m very excited for the future.”

Kiara Oguno, Junior, Middle Blocker, Thomas Jefferson

The Colonials swept their way to a National District title last week with wins over Mount Vernon, Edison and Hayfield. Oguno, who was also named district player of the year, totalled 29 kills across the three victories, hitting at an efficient .446 clip.

It’s the second District title for coach Tim Kao’s team, and the first in 13 years. The group will be carrying a 15-game winning streak into the region playoffs.

Kennedy Williams, Senior, Outside Hitter, National Cathedral

Williams had an unforgettable Senior Night last week against St. Andrew’s Episcopal. In a 3-1 win, Williams totaled 39 kills on 60 swings — an astounding 9.8 kills per set — to break the program’s single-match kills record. She also eclipsed 1,000 career kills in the victory, setting her senior season total at 431 putaways.

The Seton Hall commit is an experienced veteran on an otherwise young National Cathedral team, so coach Owen Ranger relies heavily on Williams as the team’s main source of offense. Because Williams often receives between 60 and 70 swings per match, Ranger thought she might have an outside shot at eclipsing the 1,000-kill mark at the beginning of the season.

“Everything had to break right,” Ranger said. “And then it did.”

entries.title: On Election Day, Janeese Lewis George and D.C. Voters Prepare for Change
entries.summary: Lewis George, expected to become the District’s next mayor, said she is “ready to lead and deliver.”
entries.content:
It was 336 days ago that Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George launched her mayoral campaign, offering a decidedly progressive alternative to D.C. residents after 12 years of the more centrist and business-friendly Muriel Bowser.

On Tuesday morning, Lewis George arrived at Ida B. Wells Middle School in Takoma to cast a final vote for herself.

“We're just ready to go, ready to lead and deliver for D.C. residents,” she told a gaggle of reporters.

“Yesterday I was thinking about being a young student in D.C. Public Schools,” she said. “I remember [former mayor] Sharon Pratt Kelly coming to Rudolph Elementary, and [former Ward 4 council member] Charlene Drew Jarvis. And I was thinking how blessed it is to have seen representation growing up and to believe that I could one day be able to lead my city.”

Lewis George is expected to win the mayoral race handily, but whatever celebration takes place tonight will be quickly tempered by the challenges she faces: an economic downturn, a stalled housing market, and an oft-hostile administration in the White House that may want to continue reshaping the city.

“Everything is just about building the relationships that are necessary to fight for D.C. every single day,” she said. “I've always been clear that I'm really willing to work with anyone for the benefit of D.C. residents. That includes this president and this administration. To me, it's just about being strategic, and working with your partners, and finding the things we do agree on, and double down on those things.”

Lewis George said her team has already reached out to the Trump administration and she plans to meet with the president.

“I'm looking forward to talking about how we can work together to benefit D.C. residents,” she said.

Lewis George’s supporters said they were excited to cast a ballot for her, on a day that election officials said had proceeded smoothly so far, with many polling places reporting light turnout.

“I feel like there's a lot of momentum behind her and what she stands for,” said Ward 7 resident Meredith Prescott, who also voted Tuesday at Ida B. Wells. “I think she has been a champion for climate, which is something that I feel really passionate about, and affordability in D.C. as well. It's just great to see a progressive candidate that has a lot of young people behind her and was willing to talk about things that other candidates are not.”

But not everyone is standing behind the likely mayor-to-be. Even though she recognized that Lewis George would almost certainly win on Tuesday, Mocte’Ma Robinson, 52, didn’t vote for her. The Ward 4 resident said she was concerned about the Democratic nominee’s record on public safety and questioned whether politicians who are already absorbed into the city’s political hive mind could make a real difference in the city.

“If we keep voting the same old, we’re not going to see a change,” she said.

Still, Robinson, who retired from the D.C. police department in May after 26 years, said she hopes the new city government will focus on lifting up the city’s young people, fixing dilapidated and vacant housing in the city, and better serving the city’s senior citizens. On public safety, she said she also wants to see the next mayor support the police department and strengthen a program that tries to send trained behavioral health specialists to mental-health-related 911 calls.

“We still have a mental health crisis,” she said.

Another big change Tuesday will happen on Capitol Hill, where D.C. will have a new nonvoting delegate to Congress, since Eleanor Holmes Norton — who served for three decades — decided not to run again. Robert White is likely to win the seat, though he’s facing a challenge from Republican Denise Rosado and Statehood Green Kymone Freeman.

Voters will also be choosing council members in wards 1, 3, 5 and 6, and two at-large seats. The introduction of ranked-choice voting has somewhat scrambled voting in the at-large races, where D.C. voters long had two votes to use. They still do now — kind of.

At Bancroft Elementary School in Mount Pleasant, the new ranked-choice system earned mixed reviews.

“It does give people an opportunity to select as many candidates as they like — I just don’t care for it,” said Chet Bennett, who was voting with his 85-year-old mother. “[Voting] should be in and out.”

Tom Giagtzoglou said the system allowed him to vote more freely.

“I think it enables me and other people to voice their opinion without worrying about voting for somebody that they think will win,” he said.

Council chair is also on the ballot, though incumbent Phil Mendelson is expected to cruise to victory and his 29th straight year in office.

And then there’s the ducks, of course. D.C. voters have a chance to weigh in on Initiative 86, which if passed would ban the production and sale of foie gras in the city. On Tuesday morning, Prescott said she voted in favor of the ban but did not see it as an important issue.

“It felt a little random to me that there's so much going on about that exact issue when there's a lot of other issues to focus on,” Prescott said. “I guess I'm not about force-feeding geese, so I voted yes, but it doesn't really matter too much to me.”

Some reminders for residents: Polling places in D.C. are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., and if you find yourself in line when polls are closing, you’ll still be allowed to cast a ballot. You can also leave a mail ballot at any of the 55 ballot drop boxes around the city or head to a post office — though you need to confirm that the postmark on your ballot envelope has today’s date.

Check back throughout the day for The Washington Sun’s coverage of the D.C. election and other local races.

entries.title: Morning Sun: E-Day
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Congratulations, you made it to the end of the midterms. Or, maybe just the beginning of the end. And: Check out our Election Night special coverage! Details below. 





ELECTION DAY

Closing arguments: The president vs. not-the-president. Standing near the Lincoln Memorial yesterday, Donald Trump made his final national election pitch like this: “We’ve cleaned hundreds of sites of graffiti, fixed over 2,300 lighting fixtures in Washington, D.C., cleaned and renovated over 83 statues and fountains and monuments, removed hundreds of squalid homeless encampments.”

Democrats across the country closed with if you’re tired of that, have I got a candidate for you. In Michigan, Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed tried to hit every disaffected electorate with a closing spot featuring the voice of Sen. Bernie Sanders, a lot of talk about costs and a clip from Fox News’ Jesse Watters.

El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, closed out with the gift he got Sunday from Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens. The Washington Sun’s Christa Dutton was at his final rally last night: “Our Sunday wasn’t really planned to look like it was, but someone else had enough courage to believe that that” — pointing to the American flag on the wall — “was more important than party,” Rogers said. Stevens did not actually attend the rally.

Game time has arrived.

Expectations game: Believing polls, again? “I think the biggest thing that I want to remind people now is we shouldn’t trust any polls,” Mallory McMorrow, whose Senate hopes in Michigan ended after a fake poll showed her tanking, told The Sun’s Ellie Fivas.

What about those early voting numbers everyone’s going on about? Analysts warn that the early vote has never predicted the result, The Sun’s Ayah Ali-Ahmad and Andrew Van Dam report (with charts!).

Speculation game: The world of Wednesday. What will Trump 2.0 be like if the polls are right? “The president really won’t give a fuck after November and will be focused solely on his legacy,” one Republican strategist close to the White House told The Sun. Our Ben T.N. Mause, Jasmine Wright and Joe Gould report on what people are planning for the next months or years (again, if the polls are actually right for once).

Money game: Was it worth it? OpenSecrets projects congressional races will cost about $11.9 billion — a $1.7 billion jump from 2022 after adjusting for inflation, The Sun’s Kyle Chouinard reports. Corporations and individual billionaires both spent record amounts.

Legal game: Will this midterm get decided in the courts? The Justice Department has sought to dictate how states count ballots, preemptively challenged the outcome of a Senate election and threatened election officials with prosecution. No charges have been filed, and the DOJ has lost nearly all of its legal fights so far, including at the Supreme Court, which last night declined to hear the California ballots case. The Sun’s Derek Hawkins and Adora Brown report on what might come next.

Drinking game: D.C.’s nerdiest bars tonight. The Sun’s Metro desk has a list of watering holes where you can watch returns and drink to your party’s sorrows or its good health — or possibly both, depending on the Senate map.





HOW IT WILL UNFOLD

Our guide to election night: The Sun’s Hunter Riggall and Paul Kane offer a guide to which major races to watch as the polls close. If tonight is the blue wave Democrats are hoping for, they write, control of Congress could be called by midnight. But a closer contest could mean we won’t know the balance of power for days or weeks because California and Alaska exist.

What the redistricters are watching: The Sun’s Manuela Silva has been reporting extensively on the Republican effort to redraw the House map this cycle, as well as the Democratic response, which was to also redraw.

Adam Kincaid, the executive director of the National Republican Redistricting Trust, told Manuela he’s watching North Carolina’s 1st District (aka the most expensive House race ever), Texas’ redrawn 35th, which he says is the “median of all the pickup opportunities” in the state and the margins in all the districts the Republicans redrew in Florida — especially the 14th, which includes Tampa, “a Republican district, but competitive,” he said.

John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, told Manuela to look for those East Coast redistricted seats where results could come in the fastest: the Florida races, as well as North Carolina’s 1st and 3rd districts. Another one on his list is Alabama’s 2nd District, which we told you this week could be a possible GOP dummymander.





OUR COVERAGE


The Washington Sun newsroom will be assembled tonight and posting the most interesting electoral nuggets and results on our Election Night Liveblog starting after the polls close. Some are calling it the finest dual-screen opportunity of 2026: TV on C-SPAN, phone on the blog. Know everything you need to know, plus a lot of stuff you didn’t know you needed to know.

entries.title: Welcome to the Nationals’ Fun House Offseason
entries.summary: Not fun. Fun house.
entries.content:
It would be irresponsible — intellectually, journalistically — to talk about this baseball offseason as if it is normal, though let’s try for just a minute here, as it relates to the Washington Nationals.

The Nats need competent relievers, a glaring need that could (and should) be addressed in multiple ways, including spending real money in free agency and being savvy on the margins. Their rotation could use a similar upgrade, the caveat being that it will take fewer arms to fill it out, especially since Cade Cavalli, Connelly Early and Andrew Alvarez are back.

After that, the team’s offense, a major strength in 2026, would benefit from a high-upside bat or three, extra points awarded if they can play multiple positions (think Curtis Mead, who broke out last year after arriving in a late March trade that barely nudged the Richter scale, then left in the July trade that brought Early in). A team that finishes 77-85 tends to have a good number of holes.

Now, any analysis of the Nationals short- and long-term outlook hinges on what happens with CJ Abrams. The 26-year-old, an All-Star starter this past summer, is three seasons away from reaching free agency. That means the Nats are squarely in the window of deciding whether to flip him for a massive haul while his value is sky-high.

The front office, which has been in charge for about a year, moved pitcher MacKenzie Gore for a five-player package last January. At the time, Gore was 27 and two years from free agency. No two situations are the same, nor is this winter and last winter after the Nats overachieved for more than half of 2026. The point, though, is that how the Nationals handle Abrams will be a decent bellwether for when the club plans to truly contend again. And on that front, this offseason could provide a decent bit of clarity, both with the Abrams situation and how Paul Toboni approaches the free-agent market overall.

But.

But, but, but.

It is irresponsible to talk about this baseball offseason as if it is normal. If you hadn’t heard, the sport is in the early stages of a nasty labor battle, which will almost certainly result in the owners locking out the players at midnight on Dec. 2. (Also, if you hadn’t heard that, please reach out to me with your reading and social media habits. I would like to join you under that rock.)

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

In practice, the lockout will warp the offseason to the point of being unrecognizable. Per usual, free agency opened Monday evening. But since all transactions would freeze on Dec. 2, if the lockout begins then as expected, teams have a little less than a month to sign players and make trades under the current collective bargaining agreement. After that, there’s no telling how long the lockout will last, which means the next chance to shape major league rosters will likely be in a very compressed period … under different rules … starting at an undetermined date. Fun? Not exactly. But fun house? Yes.

For Nationals fans, the added bummer is twofold, I think: After some surprising success in 2026, the team should have even more payroll flexibility than in recent winters, seeing that Stephen Strasburg’s seven-year, $245 million contract is finally finished (though in typical Lerner family fashion, there are hefty payment deferrals, meaning it’s not totally off the all-knowing books quite yet). And after Toboni and his front office spent most of last offseason remaking the major league, player development and baseball operations staffs, this would have, in a normal year, been their first crack at a full winter together.

All of this will make it harder to gauge how the new group runs an offseason that doesn’t include overhauling the organization. But in the meantime, there is a lot they can and have to do.

Late last month, the Nationals claimed right-handed reliever Braxton Roxby off waivers from the Giants and designated left-handed pitcher Zak Kent for assignment, removing Kent from the 40-man roster. Then on Sunday night, the Nats acquired infielder Nate Furman from the Giants for minor league pitcher Tony Neubeck. Furman, 25, is a left-handed hitter who fills a specific need for the Nationals, either as a fixed bench player or as a swing guy between the majors and AAA. He has three minor-league options remaining, giving the Nats a lot of roster flexibility. He’s a high-contact hitter who struggled in a tiny sample of 39 major-league plate appearances in 2026.

To make room for Furman on the 40-man roster, the Nationals cut left-handed reliever Richard Lovelady loose. The addition of Furman could also complicate infielder Jorbit Vivas’ future with the club, given their similarities as utility infielders who bat from the left side. Furman has mostly played second base in the minors (1,842 ⅓ innings) with his second-most innings at third (245).

Back in the spring, someone described Toboni, the Nationals’ president of operations, as “transaction-y.” He showed that again here, striking a deal with the Giants as they faced a significant 40-man roster crunch. By Monday evening, the Nationals had to set their 40-man roster, too, which meant removing a handful of players from it.

To do that, they placed five players on outright waivers: Lovelady, PJ Poulin and Mitchell Parker, who are all left-handed relievers, plus right-handed relievers Paxton Schultz and Ken Waldichuk. Parker was claimed by the Braves, Schultz by the Reds. Lovelady and Poulin cleared waivers and are now free agents. Waldichuk cleared and was assigned to AAA Rochester, remaining with the organization.

And then the Nats also designated infielder José Tena for assignment, ending his two-and-a-half year run with the team. In that time, Tena, who was out of minor league options, posted an adjusted OPS of 86 in 625 plate appearances. (The league average OPS+ is 100.) To get to an even 40 players, catcher Drew Millas and right-handed pitcher Matt Waldron were activated off the 60-day injured list.

With many other players getting DFA’d around the league, it will be interesting to see if the Nationals leap at any of them, which could mean more roster moves in the coming days. And soon, the Nats will choose who to protect from the Rule 5 Draft, which will trigger yet another round of 40-man shuffling.

But beyond players, the Nats have added and lost staff members on the baseball and business side, which is typical for this time of year. In the front office, Brian Rodgers is getting started as the new director of international scouting, having held that role with the Astros since 2022. For the major league staff, the Nats brought in David Besky as a pitching analyst, making that another hire from the Red Sox, Toboni’s old org.

The Nationals also lost C.J. Gillman, their director of hitting, to the Mariners, who hired him to be their major league hitting coach. That’s an immediate acknowledgement of how well their hitters performed in the majors and minors last season. It’s always a good sign when your coordinators and coaches are getting poached.

Now, for the next few weeks, we’ll see how many more transactions the Nationals will squeeze in before the end times. Another reliever — any reliever, really — would be a solid start.

entries.title: D.C. Youth Baseball Players Show Support for Coach in ICE Custody
entries.summary: Amaury Monsalve, known as “Coach A” by his players, has a reputation for instilling sportsmanship and respect for the game.
entries.content:
The detention of a D.C. youth baseball coach by Immigration and Customs Enforcement has prompted his players to speak out in support of his character.

Amaury Monsalve has been a figure in the District’s baseball community for more than two decades. He’s coached at Jackson-Reed High School, Woodson High School and, for the past three years, Alice Deal Middle School. Known simply as “Coach A,” Monsalve centers his approach on sportsmanship and respect, his players say.

Last month, he was arrested a day before a scheduled hearing regarding his removal from the country.

While driving seven people as an Uber driver on Oct. 18, D.C. Metropolitan Police stopped him for allegedly running a red light, according to a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson. Everyone in the vehicle was arrested after officers found an open alcohol container, a loaded firearm and a suspected controlled substance in the car, the spokesperson said.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

No charges were filed against Monsalve, but he was detained by ICE after a judge ordered him removed from the country at his Oct. 19 immigration hearing, a Justice Department official told The Washington Sun.

A DHS spokesperson told The Sun that Monsalve was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis in 2003 but “failed to depart as required by law.” The spokesperson added that Monsalve received a green card in 2006 but was placed in removal proceedings in March 2025 after allegedly committing fraud or willful misrepresentation to obtain a visa, other documentation or admission into the country.

Robert Carmona-Borjas, a close friend of Monsalve’s for the past 30 years who has been helping his family through his human rights nonprofit, the Arcadia Foundation, told The Sun in a statement that the issue stems from alleged omissions in immigration documentation prepared by a former attorney more than 20 years earlier, and that the judge’s order has been appealed.

Following his arrest, Monsalve has been in a Louisiana detention facility awaiting a virtual bond hearing scheduled for Tuesday in Virginia. While his wife and two children prepare for a legal battle, their community, including some of his players, has continued to support them.

Liam Novikoff plays catcher for Alice Deal Middle School’s baseball team, and last year was his first time playing for Monsalve. The team had a winning season, and the 12-year-old said he learned “valuable lessons of respect” along the way.

“He’s a great coach, and I just think he does a great job connecting with everybody on our team, because he’s just a really kind person,” Novikoff said. “He just wants to connect with everyone by acknowledging everybody’s different ways of learning and personalities.”

When Novikoff heard the news of Monsalve’s detention, he said he felt shock, sadness and anger. He’s been trying to find ways to help Monsalve’s family — and has even considered hosting a charity event.

“I was thinking of organizing a home run derby for my school to help raise awareness about what’s going on and help kind of get the word out more,” the middle schooler said. “You might have to pay to hit, or, yeah, I’ve thought of the rough draft, but I’m still in the planning area.”

One memory Novikoff shared to best describe Monsalve’s coaching style was when he made the team run laps after a win last season after his teammates made fun of the other team for sharing equipment.

“We played a team that came from a less fortunate area of D.C., and some of my teammates were talking about how the other team shared the same bats,” Novikoff said. “And after the game he pulled us all in a huddle and told us he didn’t care if we won by 20 or lost by 20; he only cared if we showed respect to the other team and how we represented our community.”

One of Novikoff’s teammates last season, Lucas Sheehy, 14, also mentioned running laps when discussing the impact Monsalve had on him as a player. “It was intense,” he said.

“Usually a coach gives up on it, like ‘one lap and now you know your lesson,’” Sheehy said. “We literally ran until some of us were so apologetic. You’ve never seen these kids be so nice to somebody. But it was definitely deserved.”

Sheehy said it encapsulated who Monsalve is as a coach and a person: not just focused on the game, but always showing up to teach the kids how to “be a human.” Lucas’ younger brother, 11-year-old Dominic, played for Monsalve’s travel team.

“Every single game, no matter if we were winning or losing, he would always just say, ‘Be a good player,’” Dominic said. “A lot of people know him as a great guy. He has great character.”

Monsalve’s wife, Aniushka, told The Sun in a statement that she has kept in contact with him while he remains in ICE custody. She said he has continued to prepare training plans for young baseball players in Venezuela as part of the program Voice of the Children, which aims to help disadvantaged children play baseball.

"My husband sees the child sitting on the bench who doesn't think he's good enough,” his wife said in the statement. “He makes it his mission to show that child that he matters and that he can succeed."
