entries.title: Will the Pollsters Get it Right?
entries.summary: The midterms have turned into a major test for polls, since some of the most consequential decisions of the cycle were made based on polling data.
entries.content:
The answer to at least one of the questions everyone has been asking will be made clear by Tuesday’s midterm results: Just how accurate were the polls?

Campaigns, donors and outside groups across the country made decisions about how to spend millions based on polls. Whether it was worth it — whether they even needed to — will soon be apparent. But because of polls, the battlegrounds that both parties are focused on are spread across far more states than at the start of the cycle.

This year’s polls have heavily favored Democratic candidates. Because of past missteps across the polling industry, polling firms have been approaching the significant leads with a lot of caution and skepticism, said Adam Carlson, a Democratic pollster. They’re also functioning in an environment with less data: there are fewer polls, and response rates have dropped.

“We're relying a lot more on vibes,” Carlson told The Washington Sun.

He added that some pollsters are so worried about being wildly off with this year’s polls — like how Democrats were inaccurately favored in 2016 — that they’re adjusting their data analysis to prevent too extreme of a tilt toward Democrats in competitive races.

“There’s a bigger reputational risk of being wrong again, underestimating Republicans or overestimating Democrats,” Carlson said.

On Monday, House Speaker Mike Johnson appeared on political commentator Scott Jennings’ radio show, where he said this cycle’s polls inaccurately favor Democrats, as they have in the past.

"The polling is wrong, OK,” Johnson said. “Everybody understands the polls have been off,” adding that polling “underrepresents Republicans.”

He said pollsters “blame Republicans” for inaccurate results.

“They say, 'Conservatives don't answer polls anymore,’” Johnson continued. “But they've learned not to trust — they don't know who that person is on the other side of the phone, and they know it's a psyop. They're trying to create this idea of a blue wave."

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

One of the issues facing pollsters is the challenge of reaching certain voters, especially those who only show up to vote in elections in which President Donald Trump is on the ballot. The Washington Post found that most Republican voters in Kansas didn’t want to speak with a pollster, while Democrats were more willing.

“They don't like the media, and they don't like pollsters,” said Charles Franklin, the director of Marquette Law School Poll. “That's a recipe that makes it especially hard to reach the very people that you most want to talk to.”

No one has to reach very far back for examples of just how wrong the polls can be. The 2026 primaries had plenty of examples: Polling found Francesca Hong, the progressive candidate in Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary, ahead by as much as 20 percentage points over the course of her campaign.

David Crowley beat her in the primary by less than 1 percentage point, wildly overperforming expectations — which were set by the polls.

The number of public polls conducted nationwide has steadily declined. According to a FiftyPlusOne analysis conducted in mid-October, there was only polling data in October for 54% of Senate races in 2026, compared to 80% of Senate races in 2018. One reason for fewer polls is because of the increasing cost to use reliable methodologies, Republican pollster Chris Wilson explained.

“Campaigns and donors and outside groups make real decisions based on those numbers,” Wilson said. “A bad poll … can move millions of dollars into a race that doesn't need it, or away from a race that does.”

Surprisingly narrow margins in this year’s polls have shifted millions toward races previously seen as safe Republican wins in the Senate, such as Mississippi and Kansas. The Democrat-aligned Senate Majority PAC dropped at least $5 million to back Adam Hamilton in Kansas and more than $1 million for Scott Colom in Mississippi.

Similarly, Republicans have stepped back from spending big in places like North Carolina and Georgia, where polls show comfortable leads for Democrats. The Senate Leadership Fund, a major Republican super PAC, originally planned to spend $18 million in North Carolina in September but entered October having spent $32 million to back Senate candidate Michael Whatley — which is when Semafor reported the super PAC planned to pull back spending. Whatley’s first ad in nearly four weeks aired only a week before Election Day.

Two firms have admitted to fabricating polling data this year, including Wedgewood Polls, which admitted online to faking polls in the Michigan Senate primary race and the Wisconsin gubernatorial race.

Michigan Democrat Mallory McMorrow, who spoke with The Washington Sun after Wedgewood revealed its fraudulent polls, said one of the reasons she suspended her primary campaign for Senate was because Wedgewood showed her with only 9% of the vote.

McMorrow said polls are closely watched by donors and national political committees. Shortly after the fake June poll, the state lawmaker said she had major donors recommending she drop out of the race, which started the “death spiral” for her campaign.

“I think the biggest thing that I want to remind people now is we shouldn’t trust any polls,” McMorrow said. “I hope this teaches us a lesson.”

Prediction market companies like Kalshi and Polymarket want to capitalize on the polling industry’s shortcomings. Rather than measuring actual voter preference data, these platforms allow users to wager money on the odds of an election result — but political operatives have warned campaigns not to build a strategy based on prediction market odds.

Pollsters should be thinking ahead to 2028, Wilson told The Sun, and figuring out ways to get the data right in two years.

“The lesson of 2026 isn’t that public opinion is unmeasurable,” Wilson said. “It’s that measuring accurately matters more than ever before.”

entries.title: Early Voting Set a Midterm Record. But Does it Matter?
entries.summary: Ballots cast before Election Day surpassed 2018 and 2022, but voting experts say it remains unclear if 2026 could match or exceed 2018’s total vote.
entries.content:
More than 57 million Americans have voted before Election Day, setting a midterm record.

As of Monday afternoon, University of Florida Election Lab figures show that — even adjusted for population growth — this cycle’s early turnout has passed 2022 and 2018, the latter of which went on to become the midterm election with the highest turnout in a century.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/g8lIj/7/Across the 27 states that report party registration, Democrats led by about 3 million ballots. Those counts show how voters are registered, not how they voted — and in several states the fastest-growing group belongs to neither major party.

But about 90% of that margin came from five states: California, Maryland, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and North Carolina — and nearly 40% of the margin is thanks to California alone. The 27 states that report party registration for early voting account for about half the national early vote, and key states such as Texas, Georgia, Michigan, New York and Ohio report no party data at all.

During the final days of early voting, the share of ballots coming from registered Democrats declined in most states where party registration is tracked.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/sG6nf/6/Only Kansas has seen a substantial reversal. Democrats led the state’s early vote by about 9,400 ballots on Oct. 28. By Monday, Republicans led by about 11,500 — a swing of nearly 21,000 in a state where the Senate race is rated by The Cook Political Report as a toss-up.

Early voting data isn’t an indicator of where the races could be headed, said Christopher Cooper, a political scientist at Western Carolina University, but they aren’t always predictive.

“It’s not the case that you can just copy and paste these results into what you’re going to see in the end,” Cooper said.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

Mail-in and in-person early voting have risen in nearly every cycle since the 1980s, said John Fortier, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a center-right think tank. Mail-in voting spiked during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and has come down since, he said. But even after falling from those heights, mail-in voting remains on a long-term upward trend.

What is shifting in 2026 is not whether Americans vote early but how — and none of that, Fortier and others cautioned, would tell you who will win.

Texans Cast 7.7 Million Early Votes

Early voting enthusiasm was clear in Texas, which wrapped up early voting with 7.7 million ballots. That early number alone nearly matches 2022’s entire vote in the state.

Almost all those votes (97%) were cast in person, largely because Texas requires voters to provide a reason to vote by mail. But it’s not just a matter of voter restrictions — Georgia and North Carolina let any voter request an absentee ballot, yet logged more than 95% of their early votes in person this year. Fortier characterized it as a regional preference, “a tradition of voting early in person,” and not a partisan one.

Early voting ran ahead of 2022 in nearly every state he analyzed, said Michael McDonald, who runs the UF Election Lab. McDonald added that registered Democrats and unaffiliated voters cast ballots faster than they did four years ago and Republican voters lagged behind their 2022 pace in some states.

That matters because breaking the early vote record is not the same as breaking the turnout record. The final numbers hinge on who shows up Tuesday, and McDonald is not sure Republicans will.

“If we don’t see Republicans get engaged at the same level as the other groups,” McDonald said, “then we may fall short of that 2018 election.”

Turnout in the predominantly Hispanic counties along the Mexican border outran the state average, he said, pointing to Hidalgo County, where about 92% of the population is Hispanic.

McDonald noted that, despite warnings of the potential presence of federal agents at polling locations, no incidents of immigration enforcement were reported at early voting sites in Hidalgo County or across the state, and Hispanic early voting ran at what he estimated was two to three times the level of prior elections.

North Carolina’s Third Bloc Surges

In North Carolina, the early vote ran well ahead of 2018 and 2022 totals. Pre-election data showed registered Democrats outpaced registered Republicans, but the fastest-growing group was voters registered with neither major party, making it hard to determine who might have the edge.

Democrats lead registered Republicans by about 345,000 ballots, about the same, proportionally, as their edge in 2018 and a substantial improvement over 2022. Since 2018, both parties have lost about four points of share to voters registered with neither party.

North Carolina finished with 2.8 million early ballots, easily surpassing its 2018 and 2022 totals.

What changed is how few of those voters were Republicans: 26%, down from 31% in 2022 and 30% in 2018.

In the previous two midterms, registered Republicans and Democrats each outnumbered North Carolinians who had registered with neither major party. This year that group passed Republicans by more than 260,000. But unaffiliated voters aren’t necessarily persuadable, Cooper said.

“Most unaffiliated voters are not swing voters,” he said. “But most swing voters are unaffiliated voters.”

Mail-in voting fell there, with about 94,000 ballots returned, down 40% from 2022. Catawba College’s Michael Bitzer pointed to “additional hurdles that the state imposed on receiving mail-in ballots,” which he told The Washington Sun meant ballots that would normally have counted did not this year.

The main one was a new requirement that voters seal an inner envelope before sealing the outer one, and failing to do so “would trigger a spoilage.”

North Carolina was an example of a national pattern. Across the 27 states and D.C. that reported both methods in each of the last two midterms, mail fell 13%, while in-person early voting rose 46%.

The decline nationwide is either pandemic habits unwinding or distrust of the Postal Service after the president’s attacks on mail voting, McDonald said, a shift The Sun reported last month among Democratic voters.

Nevada Flipped

Though Nevada's unaffiliated bloc is smaller than North Carolina's, the same reshuffling showed up there. The state counted more than 730,000 early ballots, with registered Democrats leading Republicans by about 43,000. In 2022, Republicans had been narrowly ahead.

Nearly two-thirds of those ballots came from Clark County, which holds about 70% of Nevada's registration. Jon Ralston of The Nevada Independent, who has analyzed Nevada's early returns for two decades, calls the votes banked there a Democratic "firewall." Turnout was tracking close to 2022, he said last week, but "what's not tracking is the composition of the electorate."

Georgia’s Black Turnout Increases

In Georgia, Black voters cast 32% of early votes, slightly up from 2022 and 2018. Andra Gillespie, a political scientist at Emory University, said Black voters are the largest group of Democrats in the state, and Georgia has more Republicans than Democrats overall.

If Black turnout comes in below their share — roughly 31% of registered voters, Gillespie said — Democrats cannot make up the shortfall with white, Latino or Asian American voters. Charles Bullock at the University of Georgia said that Black voters need to cast about 30% of all ballots in Georgia for it to signal a Democrat could win statewide races there.

Bullock and Gillespie flagged uneven rural turnout. Participation lagged in heavily Republican areas such as northwest and south Georgia, where Trump campaigned in the closing weeks.

entries.title: The Commanders Finally Created Some Explosive Plays in Week 8
entries.summary: Washington’s offense generated eight big plays in a 27-10 win over the Eagles.
entries.content:
The difference between wins and losses (and ties) can be as simple as this: Did you make a big play?

For the Commanders, the answer to that question has been a resounding “no” for most of this season. After four games, Washington ranked 29th in the league in explosive play rate (running plays of 10-plus yards and passing plays of 20-plus yards).

In fact, the difference between 2-4-1 and 4-2-1 could arguably be chalked up to two explosive plays that were wiped out by penalties against the Colts and 49ers.

The team has harped on generating big plays since the spring but had not been able to create them with any consistency — until Sunday. In a 27-10 win over the Eagles, the Commanders created eight explosive plays: three on the ground and five in the air. Here’s a look at how Washington was able to change its fortunes.

Commanders explosives 1 (2048x1136, AR: 1.80)
Jayden Daniels’ 14-yard scramble

If you give Daniels a free running lane, he will take it. Deep routes by Stefon Diggs, Treylon Burks and Chig Okonkwo — plus running back Austin Ekeler pulling linebacker Zack Baun (53) away from the center of the field on a flat route — left nothing but open space for Daniels.

Commanders explosives 2 (2048x1139, AR: 1.80)
Ekeler’s 18-yard rush

Not to downplay Ekeler’s efforts on this run, but it was the actions of four teammates that made this play pop. Diggs running horizontally behind the offensive line pulled corner Cooper DeJean (33) out of the play. Meanwhile, center Lucas Patrick gets enough leverage on the inner shoulder of defensive tackle Moro Ojomo to impede his angle.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Left tackle Brandon Coleman joined Okonkwo in sealing off linebacker Arnold Ebiketie. A few yards up the field, receiver Dyami Brown drove back linebacker Zack Baun, who may have found an angle before Ekeler got fully off the edge.

Commanders explosives 3 (2048x1135, AR: 1.80)
Rachaad White’s 33-yard rush

The offensive line (and tight end Ben Sinnott) also handled business on this run play. Take your pick on who to zero in on and you’ll see an Eagle defender being moved out of the way.

Of course White had to have the vision to cut back once the Eagles got leverage outside, but this was a complete blocking effort by everyone on the field. This run all but ended any chance of a last-minute comeback by Philadelphia.

Commanders explosives 4 (2048x1139, AR: 1.80)
Burks’ 21-yard catch

This was Daniels showing patience. Kurt Warner put out a video last week that harped on how Daniels can rush certain plays, which can lead him to checking down on shorter routes or not setting his feet and having passes sail on him.

With no pressure from the Eagles’ defensive line, Daniels had time to wait for Burks (furthest left) to break on his deep curl route. Once Burks separated from corner Riq Woolen, Daniels threw toward the sideline to give his receiver even more room to make the catch.

Commanders explosives 5 (2048x1143, AR: 1.79)
Diggs’ 20-yard catch

Three vertical routes by Williams, Okonkwo and Burks dragged Eagles defenders away from the middle of the field. Burks aimed his route right at safety Andrew Mukuba (24), who had given Diggs a 10-yard cushion off the line of scrimmage. With Jeremiah Trotter Jr. (bottom center) distracted by White (bottom right) coming out of the backfield, Diggs ran free on his shallow crosser.

Commanders explosives 6 (2048x1148, AR: 1.78)
Okonkwo’s 21-yard catch

On the left side of the formation, Williams and Diggs ran identical dig routes while Okonkwo ran a quick slant toward the middle of the field. On the right side, Burks ran a quick out route while Ekeler ran vertical.

Linebacker Nolan Smith (3) drops back into zone coverage at the snap and immediately puts eyes on Burks’ out route, leaving a sizable hole in the middle of the field. Okonkwo fills it immediately. Unfortunately, once he made the catch in space, Okonkwo fumbled the ball.

Commanders explosives 7 (2048x1141, AR: 1.79)
Antonio Williams’ 30-yard catch

Williams said after the game that the key to this play halfway through the fourth quarter was the safety Mukuba rolling over to cover him, leaving corner Kenny Moore II (furthest right) as the single-high safety.

Williams faked a short out route before sprinting clear past Mukuba as Moore was distracted by the twin dig routes by Diggs and Van Jefferson on the left side of the formation. By the time the ball reached Williams’ hands, he had plenty of space.

Commanders explosives 8 (2048x1147, AR: 1.79)
Burks’ 53-yard catch

Burks and Williams ran twin, double-move vertical routes on the outside with a single-high safety, Mukuba, manning the middle of the field.

A deep post route by Diggs pulled safety Marcus Epps and corner DeJean, not allowing Mukuba to commit to overhead help towards Burks or Williams, who had both beaten their coverage. Daniels dropped the ball into a pocket between Mukuba and corner Quinyon Mitchell.

Coach Dan Quinn said this play was only successful because of the 21-yard completion to Burks earlier in the game. The defense was burned by a deep comeback route, so offensive coordinator David Blough figured they would be susceptible to a fake comeback route later. He was correct.

“That's the back-and-forth that you work with in the passing game,” Quinn said on Monday. “If you get the specific looks that say, ‘Hey, here's the chance to go put the ball up.’”

entries.title: East Potomac Park Users Are Angry and Afraid Ahead of Possible Closure
entries.summary: The ongoing legal fight over Trump’s plans to expand the golf course has left cyclists, runners and others to ponder possible final days for the park.
entries.content:
It was as ideal a fall weekend as anyone in D.C. could hope for — sunny, mild and with only a light breeze — and the crowds at East Potomac Park reflected that.

Golfers played rounds on the 106-year-old municipal course as bird-watchers ambled along the perimeter with their eyes and binoculars trained on trees in the distance. A group of cyclists gathered to attempt what one admitted was a “bucket-list item” — a 100-mile ride around the island. There was a 5K run for Oakwood University’s class of 1997, fishermen cast their lines into the Washington Channel, and a group of men set up camping seats in a parking spot just to chat.

For some, it was just a chance to enjoy the beautiful fall weather. For others, it was something more.

“I’m down here because I wanted to protest this attempted takeover. I’m so angry about it. There’s so many awful things that this administration is doing, but this cuts somehow differently,” said Krista Riddley, a Maryland resident and member of the DMV Caribbean Ridazz cycling club.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

But Riddley’s anger over President Donald Trump’s plans to close East Potomac Park so he can renovate the golf course — and in the process largely demolish Ohio Drive, the perimeter road popular with runners, walkers, cyclists and drivers looking to access Hains Point, the picturesque southern tip of the island — also mixed with another emotion: an unplanned desire to say goodbye.

“I was like, ‘I’ve got to do some laps because I don’t know when this is going to end,’” she said.

Those sometimes conflicting emotions — simmering anger and wistful sadness — have only become more pronounced over the last week, as Trump has barreled forward with his plans to close East Potomac Park on Nov. 15 to “build a World Class Championship Golf Course on the site of the current East Potomac Golf Links,” as he wrote on Truth Social last month.

The popular golf course seems likeliest to shutter that day; the National Park Service recently announced it had severed its partnership with the nonprofit National Links Trust to operate the course. But whether Trump manages to close off all of East Potomac Park to its many other users remains an unsettled question, and one that’s currently fueling activism and the legal fight waged against it.

“The goal right now is to make sure it doesn’t get shut down,” said Rebecca Miller, the executive director of the D.C. Preservation League, one of the plaintiffs in ongoing litigation over Trump’s ever-evolving plans for the island. To that end, her attorneys are planning to ask for a temporary restraining order this week in hopes of keeping public access to East Potomac Park while the legal battle plays out.

The growing expectation that Trump will engineer a way to close East Potomac, regardless of residents’ best efforts, brought hundreds of people to the park on Saturday for a protest organized by the Washington Area Bicyclist Association.

Hains Point East Potomac protest (7008x4672, AR: 1.50)
Protesters held signs — “Don’t Oligarchize East Potomac,” “Corrupt (Tiny) Hands Off Hains Point,” “No Gilded Golf Course” and “Golf Balls Don’t Hurt People, Selfish Presidents Do” — and wore costumes, both to make a point and to celebrate Halloween. One woman was a “park deranger” with the “National Park Disservice,” a man with an oversized 20-pound Trump head drew laughs and boos, and there were multiple people dressed up like the Lorax, a famed Dr. Seuss character who “speaks for the trees.”

“I think this is pretty on the nose for all the trees coming down, so I wanted to speak for them,” said Hannah Dighton, a D.C. resident, triathlete, and Lorax, referencing the recent felling of hundreds of trees by the National Park Service that drew an angry rebuke from the federal judge overseeing the lawsuit against Trump’s plans.

One protest sign read: “I’m the Lorax who speaks for the trees, which you seem to be chopping as fast as you please! Unless someone like you cares a whole awful lot, nothing is going to get better. It’s not.”

Over the weekend, park users conceded one point made by Trump: East Potomac needs work, notably the seawall surrounding the island. It is slowly sinking, leading to flooding during periods of heavy rainfall or high tides.

“You can repair the seawall, you can close off Hains Point temporarily to make things safer, but you don’t have to turn the park into a one-use location after that,” said Megan Jones, an Arlington resident and longtime cyclist who from 2012 to 2019 organized an annual New Year’s Day 100-mile ride around the island.

According to a filing with the National Capital Planning Commission late last week, fixing the seawall alone would cost $304.5 million and take between two and a half and three and a half years to complete. Critics of Trump’s plan say the investment would make more fiscal sense if he kept the park open to all users and didn’t just limit it to those who would play on the planned 18-hole golf course.

“I fully support the fixing of the seawall if the property remains for how it’s used today,” said Alex Dickson, a local golfer, publisher of Beltway Golfer, and one of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit to stop Trump from moving forward with plan to build a course that takes up the entire island. “Cyclists, walkers, barbecuers, people partying, the fishermen — are going to be pissed. A lot of people use this place.”

Hains Point East Potomac Park (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)
Ashley Krupa is one of them, and on Sunday she helped organize her cycling club’s second 100-mile ride around East Potomac Park. “This year with the potential closure it attracted a lot more people,” she said. “We wanted to do it before we lose access.”

Mayor Muriel Bowser has struck a diplomatic tone on the issue of what should come of East Potomac Park, though on Monday she made clear that she wants some type of roadway like Ohio Drive to remain in any future iterations of the island.

“I think we should think about it not necessarily as a road as it is now, but a recreational use road that would accommodate people having access to the park, would accommodate people riding bikes, and pushing strollers and jogging and having a place to walk to get to the playgrounds and other facilities that can be there,” she said. “I think the bottom line is that the park accommodates a great golf course now. Do we want a world-class golf course? Yes, but we think that it can and should accommodate other uses."

Alex Cohen, the D.C. resident behind the Save East Po campaign, says he doesn’t want people to be resigned to the fact that East Potomac will close on Nov. 15. “People that say they don't care about politics. I appreciate that, but politics is coming for them and their literal places of recreation,” he said.

To that end, the Washington Area Bicyclist Association is hosting a congressional lobby day on Nov. 12 to oppose any further funding for Trump’s plans for East Potomac Park. Davey Hearn, a local cyclist who drew widespread attention after federal prosecutors unsuccessfully tried to go after him for what Trump said was vandalism of the Reflecting Pool, said more needs to be done.

“Maybe we can have a 24/7 vigil with bikers and runners here in the critical period approaching Nov. 15,” he said at Saturday’s rally. “We’re not going to put up with this. We know it’s going to be a long fight, but we have to be ready for the long haul.”

Dickson agreed. “November 15 might come, but you’ve got to keep fighting. If the bulldozers come out in December, you’ve got to keep fighting. If they rip up Ohio Drive in February, you gotta keep fighting,” he said. “Don’t stop fighting.”

entries.title: Where Does Trump Go From Here?
entries.summary: “The president really won’t give a fuck after November and will be focused solely on his legacy,” said one Republican strategist close to the White House.
entries.content:
Few people outside of President Donald Trump know what his plans are after Election Day.

But aides, operatives and strategists are gaming out what a potential lame-duck Congress would prioritize for the final weeks of Republican control under Trump. Outside groups are readying for a potential push for a new Supreme Court justice should Republicans retain the Senate. And the administration is preparing for two years of investigations, pardons and executive actions that are expected to shape Trump’s presidential legacy.

“The president really won’t give a fuck after November and will be focused solely on his legacy,” one Republican strategist close to the White House told The Washington Sun.

The Sun spoke with over a dozen aides, party strategists and operatives who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private deliberations. Allies say they expect the White House and Republican lawmakers to focus on making permanent changes that have been made during Trump’s first two years back in the White House — something they said the Biden administration didn’t do.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

As the country’s domestic economic issues and geopolitical entanglements have proven difficult to solve, Trump has instead put outsize focus on beautification projects in Washington. He returned Monday to the site of one of his most high-profile projects — the Reflecting Pool at the Lincoln Memorial — for a final speech before voters head to the polls.
Trump 26306692908991 (1024x682, AR: 1.50)The president’s intense pursuit of the projects — including building a White House ballroom, a reimagining of the East Potomac Golf Links and plans for an arch in front of Arlington National Cemetery that would dwarf France’s Arc de Triomphe — would be a marker of his final two years in office, even if completing them might mean flouting court orders.

As Trump indulges his desire to build things, his administration will be bracing for a wave of investigations that Democrats have promised to undertake if they wrest control of one or both congressional chambers. When Democrats took control of the House after the midterms in Trump’s first term, inquiries and investigations into Rudy Giuliani’s activities in Ukraine led to the first of two impeachments brought against Trump.

Allies believe Trump and his administration are better prepared this time to push back more forcefully.

“The more radical wing of the [Democratic] Party is going to demand investigations and impeachment,” said a source close to Trump, who added that it would likely spark the president “to demand his Justice Department do the same.”

In a statement to The Sun, the White House noted Trump’s rallies have highlighted what his administration has done for voters.

“These armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation to Fake News Washington Sun have no idea what they’re talking about,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. “The president will continue advancing his proven, commonsense agenda to accelerate growth, create jobs, and lower costs for Americans. The best is yet to come.”

The White House has been preparing for the possibility of the House flipping to the Democrats since earlier this year, as previously reported by The Sun. Federal agencies sent an email last week, according to two sources familiar with the outreach, reminding political appointees that the agencies are paying part of their professional liability insurance, as stipulated under federal law.

Should Democrats gain congressional power, Trump allies say they anticipate the president will lean even more heavily on executive actions and dole out even more pardons. Multiple pardon advocates told The Sun that the White House has been considering issuing another batch of clemencies following the midterms, though the advocates said it was unclear whether their clients would receive one.

Those under consideration, according to three people familiar with the discussions, included those accused or charged with white-collar crimes that the White House sought to avoid pardoning before the elections.

The Sun previously reported that the White House is weighing mass pardons for junior staff. In an interview with the New York Post published on Monday, Trump indicated he would pardon allies such as Elon Musk and others if Democrats target them with investigations, saying, “That’s what [former President Joe] Biden did.”

Asked if he’d do it for everybody who worked for him, Trump said he wouldn’t even need to think about it.

“I did it for J6,” he said, referring to granting clemency to roughly 1,600 people involved in the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol.

A loss of control in either congressional chamber after Tuesday’s races would leave the White House with less than two months to legislate with the Republican trifecta. Priorities for a lame-duck Congress, though, remain largely unchanged from before Congress recessed for the election’s stretch run and include government and military funding, permitting reform and a party-line reconciliation package.
Trump 26305776560788 (1024x682, AR: 1.50)The Senate is expected to pick back up permitting reform when it returns regardless of what happens, a senior Republican aide told The Sun.

Sources close to the White House say the permitting reform negotiations and eventual vote could be a preview of how top Democrats, especially those in the House under Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become House speaker should Democrats take control, would work with the White House going forward.

Trump said he would become “Mr. Veto” with them in charge.

“I’m not going to let them ruin it,” he told the New York Post. “And then, at some point, we’ll probably make deals.”

The senior Republican aide said that a successful vote on permitting reform would also be a win for Democrats because it would eat up floor time and limit legislative time on other Republican priorities, such as its reconciliation process that lawmakers are using to cover part of Trump’s $1.5 trillion defense budget request.

With lawmakers facing a Dec. 11 government funding deadline, Congress could extend its stopgap funding measure into 2027, essentially leaving a wartime Pentagon to operate at existing funding levels.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has publicly insisted that the administration remains committed to securing at least $350 billion through the party-line reconciliation process. But the proposal made little headway, and Congress will have little time when it returns — 20 legislative days in the House and 22 in the Senate before the end of the year.

“Publicly, they are pushing for $350 billion in reconciliation,” said a defense lobbyist speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter. “Privately, the Pentagon knows it’s not going to happen. They have to shift some into the base bill and maybe a small supplemental.”

Still, Republicans on the Senate Armed Services Committee are developing their own reconciliation proposal, two people familiar with the effort told The Sun. The previously unreported work appears intended to give congressional Republicans a greater say in which programs get added funding.

The Defense Department is also revisiting its fiscal year 2027 spending plans and reconciliation proposal, one of the people said — an acknowledgement that the department’s original proposal is in doubt.

Those alternatives don’t appear on a glide path to passage, either. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), an appropriator, predicted at an event last week that Congress would extend the continuing resolution into January or February. He warned that Democrats, if they regain control of Congress, could condition defense funding on restrictions against continued military operations in Iran.

If lawmakers were to punt even further, a year-long continuing resolution could leave defense spending about $250 billion below the administration’s request for fiscal year 2027.

“I have no confidence that appropriations or reconciliation gets done,” the lobbyist said.

Should Republicans lose the Senate in addition to the House, a third, more ambitious reconciliation bill could emerge.

“If we lose both chambers, I think it’s going to be, like, the mother of all reconciliation bills,” the senior Republican aide said.

A potential bill could include money to fund the government through the end of Trump’s second term and raise the debt ceiling to remove Democratic leverage, the aide added.

One Republican operative described the more robust reconciliation bill as a last-gasp vehicle to push to pass before losing control of legislating in January.

“Throw every fucking thing they can in there,” they said, calling it a “Chipotle fucking burrito bill.”

Thomas 26180691089064 (1024x682, AR: 1.50)
Beyond policymaking, there’s also expected to be discussion about shoring up future control of the Supreme Court. Outside groups, a strategist close with the White House said, are already discussing how to nudge Justice Clarence Thomas to step down and make Trump’s last two years about the court.

Thomas and Justice Samuel Alito are the high-court’s oldest sitting justices at 78 and 76 years old, respectively.

Many aides, staffers and operatives who spoke with The Sun were hesitant to make firm predictions about what the administration would do after Election Day. It could all change, they said, based on the unpredictable president’s reaction to the electoral results. The post-midterms landscape, those people said, would appear similar to how the Republican Party has charted its course for the past decade, guided by Trump’s whims.

“I don’t think anybody who tells you they know what’s going to happen has any idea what they’re talking about,” the source close to Trump said. “He’s extraordinarily unpredictable.”

entries.title: These Early-Closing States Could Show Where Election Night Is Headed
entries.summary: Polls will start closing at 6 p.m. ET. These races could provide early clues about which party is having a good night.
entries.content:
Control of Congress may not be determined for hours, days or even weeks after Election Day. But polls will begin closing at 6 p.m. ET. Here are the races to watch early in the evening that may indicate how the results play out.

After 6 p.m.

Kentucky: Polls in eastern Kentucky will close at 6 p.m. ET, tied for the earliest in the country.

The earliest relevant returns, then, could come out of Kentucky’s 6th District, based in Lexington. The 6th went for President Donald Trump by 15 percentage points in 2024, but national Democrats are targeting it anyway and The Cook Political Report has rated it a “toss-up.” The seat is open as incumbent Republican Rep. Andy Barr runs to succeed Mitch McConnell in the Senate.

After 7 p.m.

Virginia: Keep an eye on the battleground 1st and 2nd Congressional Districts.

The 1st is considered the true toss-up: Republican Rep. Rob Wittman has represented the Northern Neck region for close to two decades and was reelected in 2024 by a double-digit margin. If Wittman is in trouble, the GOP could be in for a long night.

Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans is considered more imperiled in the coastal 2nd District, which in the past decade has gone from red to blue and back to red again. If Kiggans’ race is called against her quickly, keep an eye on the 5th District along the commonwealth’s southwestern corner, because if that Trump +12 seat is close, it’s going to be a very long night for Republicans.

Florida: The 14th and 22nd Congressional Districts were redrawn to favor Republicans earlier this year as part of the redistricting wars, but both are considered toss-ups. If Tuesday turns into a blue wave, those new maps could backfire.

The Tampa-based 14th is represented by Rep. Kathy Castor and was redrawn to add rural areas in eastern and southern Hillsborough County.

The 22nd stretches from western Palm Beach County across the Everglades to Marco Island on the Gulf Coast. Trump would have won it by 11 percentage points in 2024 but would have lost it by 3 percentage points in 2020. The Republican candidate has spent heavily on TV advertising in lieu of in-person campaigning.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

Rep. María Elvira Salazar’s Miami-based 27th District remains largely unchanged under the new map but will also be under the microscope. Salazar has been one of the loudest Republicans critiquing Trump’s immigration crackdown.

South Carolina: Polling indicates Democrat Annie Andrews has a chance of scoring an upset win over Republican Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the late Lindsey Graham, in a state Trump won by 18 percentage points two years ago.

Black voters accounted for almost 30% of early voting, a large enough share that could boost Andrews. Graham, a political newcomer, has been buoyed by two October visits from Trump.

Georgia: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is favored to win reelection over his Republican opponent, Rep. Mike Collins.

A key question is whether his coattails can help Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms make history and become the nation’s first Black woman to be elected governor. Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, is locked in a tight race with Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire health care executive who has spent more than $200 million of his own money on his campaign.

After 7:30 p.m.

Ohio: Democrat Sherrod Brown is mounting a competitive comeback bid against Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Some Republicans worry Husted could be dragged down by gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who is trailing in polls against Democrat Amy Acton.

Congressional races in Districts 7, 9, 10 and 15 are also considered competitive.

North Carolina: Republicans have held the 11th congressional district in western North Carolina since 2013. But political operatives of both parties believe the district of outgoing Rep. Chuck Edwards is leaning Democratic this cycle.

North Carolina’s 1st District is also considered a toss-up, even after it was redrawn to be more conservative earlier this year. Democratic Rep. Don Davis is looking to defend his seat from a Trump-backed challenger in the northeastern part of the state.

The rest of the night … and after

After 8 p.m. ET, polls will close in more than a dozen states, and continue to close for hours thereafter. In the competitive state of Alaska, polls will close at midnight ET.

If Tuesday is the blue wave Democrats are hoping for, control of Congress could be called by midnight. But a closer contest could mean we won’t know the balance of power for days or weeks. Counting in California is famously slow because most voters there cast ballots by mail, and the state has two Republican seats that could swing to the Democrats.

Results are also slow to come out of Alaska, where a crucial Senate race is on the ballot.

entries.title: The Election Day Legal Stress Test Is Finally Here
entries.summary: There’s uncertainty about how the election might spill into courts, but state officials are anticipating something.
entries.content:
After months of litigation and speculation, Election Day could finally test how the Trump administration will use the legal system to influence the outcome of the midterms.

In the run-up to Tuesday, the Justice Department has sought to dictate how states count ballots, preemptively challenged the outcome of a Senate election and threatened election officials with prosecution.

The administration has lost nearly all of its legal fights so far, and no charges have been brought. But President Donald Trump and DOJ officials have set the stage for more potential legal showdowns over the results or what occurs at polling locations.

The last time Trump was in power during a nationwide federal election, in 2020, he and an army of allies tried to overturn his loss to President Joe Biden — an effort that was resoundingly shot down in court.

He referenced that election in a Saturday social media post in which he also complained about a recent court ruling and falsely claimed that the top U.S. attorney in California had found millions of “illegal Votes.”

“We are going to continue our yearslong fight on Election Integrity,” Trump posted.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

The Trump administration has pointed the DOJ's immense resources at the states over the past 18 months in attempts to nationalize critical aspects of election administration, which, under the Constitution, is the primary responsibility of the states.

They have pressed unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud and security vulnerabilities in lawsuits to obtain voter rolls that have been widely unsuccessful and an executive order on mail ballots that was stopped in litigation.

The administration has faced pushback from many state and local officials — some of whom have essentially taken to treating the federal government like an adversary instead of the partner it has been in elections past. There’s uncertainty about how the election might spill into the courts, but they are anticipating something.

“Our election officials are concerned about the federal government overstepping their role,” said Tammy Patrick, the chief program officer for the nonprofit National Association of Election Officials. “These are election officials all across the country — state and local, Republican, Democrat, elected, appointed, hired.”

Democrats and voting rights groups already have asked courts to stop federal law enforcement, the National Guard and immigration agents from going to polling locations. California Gov. Gavin Newsom went farther.

“A warning to Donald Trump: I’m deploying election lawyers to key battleground districts in California to protect every vote. And I just made it a FELONY to illegally seize ballots,” Newsom said.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones launched a Voter Protection Section, a team of lawyers to enforce voting rights laws and investigate threats to the ballot. And New York’s attorney general, Letitia James, emphasized that this year’s Election Protection Hotline is intended to “ensure that our elections remain free from intimidation and harassment.”

In Washington, FBI officials instructed agents to stay away from polling places after videos surfaced on social media showing National Guard troops and agents from Trump’s D.C. law enforcement task force standing outside places where Washingtonians were voting. The directive was disclosed in a lawsuit against the federal government over alleged plans to dispatch ICE agents to polling sites.

Election experts say they believe state and local officials are well equipped to resist any unlawful federal incursions on Election Day and that courts will continue to rule against the administration if it overreaches.

“I guarantee you, the state attorneys general are very prepared, and everyone is going to work collectively, Republican and Democrat alike, to protect state sovereignty over their elections process and protect the chain of custody of ballots,” said David Becker, a former attorney in the DOJ’s Voting Section who now runs the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research. “And I'm very confident that's going to continue through Election Day.”

The Trump administration has shown it is ready to litigate. In Alaska, a lawsuit laid the groundwork for challenging the outcome of Alaska’s Senate race but has been thrown out. The administration has vowed to appeal, and some Republicans have raised the possibility of blocking Democrat Mary Peltola from being seated if she wins.

In California, the U.S. Supreme Court quickly denied the DOJ’s request for the justices to force the state to set aside 20,000 ballots it claims may be from noncitizens. Multiple lower judges have blocked the administration’s bid to prevent the disputed ballots from being counted. But the department has sent grand jury subpoenas to election officials in the state in connection with its voter roll investigation, with instructions to appear for a proceeding on Wednesday morning.

“We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced,” Acting Attorney General Trent McCotter said of the litigation Wednesday on social media.

The DOJ says it’s also deploying 1,000 election monitors across the country, hundreds more than in any previous election. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon has said they will be tasked with looking for cases of alleged fraud in addition to their normal assignment of passively watching for compliance with voting rights laws.

In his second term, Trump has reshaped the Justice Department by appointing his former criminal lawyer, Todd Blanche, as attorney general, installing other loyalists in senior roles, and purging thousands of career attorneys and staffers. The Civil Rights Division has lost hundreds of employees under Trump, and nearly all of the Voting Section’s attorneys have turned over, many of them replaced by lawyers with Trumpworld bona fides and virtually no experience with elections.

On the sidelines, a chorus of election deniers with close ties to Trump are boosting the administration’s claims and fanning false conspiracy theories about the nation’s voting systems. Among them is Ed Martin, the former interim U.S. attorney in Washington, who left the DOJ over the summer to focus on what Trump said would be election “legal battles.”

Also joining the fray is Tina Peters, a former Colorado election clerk who served time in prison for her involvement in a breach of her county’s voting system. She claimed she met with Trump last month to encourage him to use federal law enforcement officers to investigate vote counting.

On Sunday night, the Senate Democratic Caucus heard from leading Democratic election attorney Marc Elias about pending litigation, anticipated legal challenges and how to counter potential election interference, according to a Senate Democratic aide.

The discussion focused specifically on the heightened threat of election issues in key Senate battleground states, where MAGA-aligned Republicans hold power at the state or local level, the aide said.

It's an atmosphere of distrust and a sharp partisan split ahead of a midterm election that will determine which party controls the House and Senate, one in which the Trump administration has pushed aggressively on election system overhauls.

Several former DOJ officials with expertise in election issues said the DOJ may continue to file legal challenges once polls close. But they emphasized that they viewed the administration’s sweeping attempts to tighten its grip as desperation rather than a coherent strategy.

“I don’t have concerns about voters not being able to go out and vote safely. Those ballots will be counted,” said Eileen O’Connor, a former trial attorney in the DOJ’s Voting Section who manages the Brennan Center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program. “My concern is more of the same — attempting to undermine confidence and just injecting more chaos. That’s what all of this is anyway.”

“The states are responding as they should, but this is not a position they should be in,” she added. “They shouldn’t have to be wasting all these resources fighting the federal government. They’re doing what they have to do.”

To date, the administration’s attempts to intervene in state election affairs have been almost entirely unsuccessful in court.

Executive orders Trump issued on proof-of-citizenship and mail-ballot restrictions have been blocked in court. The administration has lost 27 of 31 lawsuits it brought against states and Washington, D.C., seeking to force them to hand over sensitive voter data. A subpoena for poll worker data was quashed in Georgia.

Becker, of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said, “They have an unprecedented, unblemished record of failure.”

entries.title: ‘Unprecedented’: Election Spending Breaks Records — and Standards
entries.summary: Billionaires, corporations, AI and regulatory rot are playing leading roles in the upheaval.
entries.content:
This will be the most expensive midterm election in American history — and won’t be close.

Nonpartisan research organization OpenSecrets projects congressional races will cost about $11.9 billion, which represents a $1.7 billion jump from 2022 after adjusting for inflation.

A confluence of factors — including politically motivated billionaires, artificial intelligence advances and a hobbled campaign finance regulation system — have contributed to a laissez-faire environment unlike any in modern U.S. history.

Big money gets bigger

Contributing to the top-line election spending number are corporations and individual billionaires, both spending record amounts this cycle.

For corporate America, the boost has come on the back of the cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence and gaming industries, which, along with private equity, venture capital and energy interests, have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into House and Senate races.

That includes at least $653.9 million worth of direct corporate contributions, according to OpenSecrets.

Then there’s the rocket-sized elephant in the room: Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and a key ally of President Donald Trump.

By The Guardian’s count, Musk has spent $446 million, or just under 4% of OpenSecrets’ projected total for the entire midterm election.

Much of Musk’s spending has centered on the U.S. Senate race in Texas, where his spaceflight and technology company, SpaceX, is headquartered.

Brendan Fischer, director of strategic investigations at the Campaign Legal Center, said he knows of no parallel in modern American history to Musk’s political spending.

Political megadonors aren’t new, and “there’s always been at least one donor” who stood out each cycle, he said.

“But, to my knowledge, none of those top megadonors in past election cycles had given such a substantial portion of the overall fundraising,” Fischer said. “The amounts that were eye popping at the time … appear pretty modest in retrospect.”

Other prominent megadonors this election cycle include conservative businesswoman Miriam Adelson, wife of the late casino mogul Sheldon Adelson, and liberal billionaire George Soros.

“The reason we really care about money in politics is not necessarily just because of what happens on Election Day,” Fischer said, “but what happens after elected officials supported by that money take office. It’s the question of who they’re going to be accountable to.”

Craig Holman, a lobbyist for progressive think tank Public Citizen, believes there’s a relationship between the Trump administration’s entanglement of public and private interests and the massive uptick in corporate spending. Holman also thinks that’s readily apparent through Musk, who led the agency-slashing Department of Government Efficiency early in Trump’s second term.

“One person having such a profound influence on the election is unprecedented,” said Brendan Glavin, director of insights at OpenSecrets.

Going artificial

Along with the artificial intelligence industry’s heavy involvement, technology is changing the way campaigns and prospective voters operate.

In campaign advertising — which collectively cost $11.6 billion this cycle at the state and federal levels, according to AdImpact — committees are turning to AI to show opponents saying or doing things that never actually happened.

Last month, Wesleyan Media Project announced that it had tracked $137 million spent on ads generated “at least in part” through AI.

“It’s just a total fraud against the American voters,” Holman said. “We need to have disclosure anytime that type of ‘deep fake’ is used by a campaign.”

There is no federal standard for disclosing AI use in political ads, although more than 30 states have passed AI-related regulations for political advertising as of June, according to law firm Wiley Rein.

Brian Ruddle, vice president of political affairs at conservative media and campaign firm Harris Media Group, is also seeing campaigns adapt to some voters turning to AI chatbots for election information.

While only 8% of voters have used chatbots to research elections, according to Pew Research Center, Ruddle said some larger campaigns are ensuring that their websites are “easily crawlable by AI systems.” That could mean popular chatbots more regularly return results from political campaigns.

But the strategy could be even more effective in smaller races that don’t have the same volume of information online about them, Ruddle said.

“Some campaigns have caught on” to adapting to AI, he said. “Some haven’t.”

‘No cop on the beat’

The Federal Election Commission, which enforces and regulates the nation’s campaign finance laws, has been severely hobbled since May 2025 because it doesn’t have enough commissioners.

Currently, the commission has two members (both of whom are Democrats) but that’s not enough to hold hearings, issue advisory opinions or approve enforcement actions. Trump has nominated two Republicans who would provide a minimum quorum of four, but neither have been confirmed by the U.S. Senate.

The FEC is “sitting there doing nothing. It’s received over 300 complaints and nothing is done on those complaints,” Holman said. “We have a Trump administration that's particularly susceptible to influence peddling by the big spenders, and we have no cop on the beat.”

Because of that lack of quorum, the FEC is unable to establish an “easy fix” for social media influencers not disclosing when they’re being paid by political interests, Fischer said. Commissioners would, however, still have to exert the will to get that done even with four members, he noted.

With elections looming, Holman said, “there are going to be so many more abuses that the Federal Election Commission should be right on top of."

entries.title: U.S. Conducts Defensive Strikes on Iranian Targets in the Strait of Hormuz
entries.summary: A U.S. official told the AP that the target was "Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets."
entries.content:
The United States has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, a U.S. official said Monday, on the eve of crucial midterm elections.

A U.S. official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said the U.S. conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz. “Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets” were targeted, he said Monday.

Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island.

The strikes, which appeared to be limited as opposed to a full return to hostilities, came on the eve of crucial American midterm elections. President Donald Trump has previously said the U.S. wouldn’t launch strikes on Iran before the midterms.

The unpopular Iran war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.

Vice President JD Vance told reporters earlier Monday that he just spoke to Trump about talks with Iran and said that “the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”

entries.title: Justice Department Bars Jack Smith From Testifying in Trump’s BBC Lawsuit
entries.summary: The BBC wants to question the former special counsel about the president’s role in Jan. 6.
entries.content:
The Justice Department has refused to give former special counsel Jack Smith permission to testify in President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

The broadcaster wants to question Smith about evidence he gathered while investigating Trump’s efforts to contest the 2020 election, but in a letter filed Monday night, the Justice Department said that could expose grand jury secrets and classified information, and argued Smith’s knowledge of the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol was “secondhand.”

“Any purported ‘need’ for such second-hand knowledge cannot outweigh the Department’s significant interest in preserving the confidentiality of materials subject to law enforcement privilege and executive privilege,” Justice Department lawyer Pardis Gheibi wrote.

Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett has already ruled that Smith has information relevant to Trump’s speech on Jan. 6 and the subsequent Capitol attack.

Trump sued the BBC in December over a documentary that combined two parts of his speech that preceded the Capitol riot, alleging the BBC’s edit falsely suggested he encouraged the attack. The BBC argued Smith’s evidence could show that Trump helped cause the violence.

The BBC has turned the lawsuit against Trump into an opportunity to seek records as part of the discovery process.

The broadcaster also noted that the Justice Department allowed Smith to testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee last month.

entries.title: ‘Prepare Yourself’: Election Day Doomsday Messages Hit a Crescendo
entries.summary: Trump and Republicans are sounding alarms in fundraising emails. Democrats often take a different approach.
entries.content:
The message from President Donald Trump is grim.

"What I’m about to share with you is emotional. Prepare yourself,” he tells supporters.

Trump then declares: “This could be my final week as President.”

Of course, Trump has no plans to resign his office now or any time during the next two years of his second term, all while he openly muses about running — unconstitutionally, almost certainly — for a third term.
Trump.email.message (418x364, AR: 1.15)But recent emails and texts from Republican political committees — many paid for by a Trump-controlled fundraising committee known as the Trump National Committee JFC — are serving up hyperbolic Hail Marys in an effort to scare supporters into voting, donating and stemming a Republican electoral bloodbath that leads to Democrats controlling Congress.

Harsh language meant to incite fear and unease has become a hallmark of Republican emails in recent weeks as more polls show a Democratic majority is within reach.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is warning against “one of the most dangerous Democrats running anywhere in America” by urging his supporters to stop Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for the Senate in Michigan, in an email sent during the early hours of Monday morning.

El-Sayed’s campaign got a $2.4 million boost after Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Michigan) endorsed his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, according to The Washington Post. 

Cruz characterizes El-Sayed as a “radical socialist with ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.” In the email accessed through politicalemails.org, Cruz called on “fellow conservatives” to stop El-Sayed from “gaining access to our top national security secrets.”

Peter Loge, the director of the Project on Ethics in Political Communication at George Washington University, said the “vote for the lesser of two evils” approach no longer applies, and Republicans have adopted a "vote against the evil of two lessers” mindset.

“Republicans aren't saying, ‘Vote for us. We're doing great.’ They're saying, ‘Vote against them because you should be afraid of them,’” Loge said.

Cruz has been warning since January what a Democratic majority could mean for the Republican Party. In a phone call with donors, Cruz said he told Trump, “You're going to lose the House, you're going to lose the Senate, you're going to spend the next two years being impeached every single week,” amid rising costs and tariffs, Axios reported.

Cruz’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Another senator joining Cruz is Sen. Tim Scott (R- South Carolina).

“If we lose this race, Republicans are DONE,” Scott wrote in an Oct. 7 email from his political committee. Scott said that contributions to his “emergency fund” would aid Republican victories in Texas, Maine, Georgia, Minnesota and Ohio, helping the party retain the Senate majority.

Scott is the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. Scott’s communications director referred The Sun to public relations professional Nathan Brand from On Brand Strategies, who in turn referred The Sun to the NRSC, which acknowledged questions but did not otherwise answer them.

In recent weeks, emails paid for by Tim Scott for America have sent Maine and Minnesota warnings, and another email predicted that “the fate of Texas” hinged on a response to the email.“

Ken Paxton is in TROUBLE!” it said of the Republican U.S. Senate candidate running in Texas against Democrat James Talarico.

Democratic senators are largely appealing to voters’ anger in their last-minute messaging — sometimes with a dash of fear salted in.

Sen. Jon Ossoff, for one, sent an email Monday morning saying the midterms are the “last chance to stop MAGA,” and if Georgia is lost, “we can wave goodbye to any chance of taking back the Senate.”

Ossoff says the immediate answer to outrage about the state of the country is donating to his reelection campaign, where he is running against Republican Rep. Mike Collins.

In a speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday afternoon, Trump said the Democratic candidates this cycle are “the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history” with the most “radical agenda.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump continued.

Trump’s email messaging Monday mirrored that sentiment. One message read like a middle schooler’s social media post as the president asks his “real ones” to stand by him during a “heartbreaking” time — and questioned his supporters on whether they’ve “canceled on the MAGA movement?”

Trump then asks for money: “Any amount, even a small gift, tells them the patriots who started this with me in 2016 are still standing.”

In another email last week, Trump described a night reflecting in prayer at the White House Rose Garden.

“From our cities to the countryside, dangerous socialists and communists are preparing to destroy our Republican Majorities in the House and the Senate,” he wrote to supporters.

Loge said fear drives voters because they’re “more afraid of losing things than they are motivated by gaining things.”

While Democrats often appeal to voters’ sense of justice, Loge said Republicans’ eleventh-hour messaging is predictable because the Trump and MAGA brand involves being “angry” and “afraid.”

“Voters will say, ‘You know what? I'm angry, I'm afraid. I'm also tired, and I want a better tomorrow. So I'm going to go for a candidate who says they're going to fix things and bring a better tomorrow,’” Loge said.

entries.title: DOJ Sent Poll Monitors Largely to Democratic, Diverse Areas
entries.summary: Data analysis shows the DOJ’s increased Election Day monitoring effort focused on places with more immigrants and minority voters.
entries.content:
The Justice Department’s expanded effort to send monitors to polling places is landing in Democratic-leaning areas, with a focus on counties with higher immigrant populations and minority voters.

An analysis from The Washington Sun found the county deployments in about 125 jurisdictions in all 50 states look more partisan than the prior two elections. In 2022, when monitors were sent to 24 states, their typical destination county supported Harris by 9 percentage points. In 2024, when monitors were sent to 27 states, their typical destination supported Harris by 12 percentage points. In 2026, that figure would be 16 percentage points.

The federal government waited until Election Day to announce the jurisdictions where it is sending monitors. Although the Justice Department has for decades sent attorneys to ensure compliance with voting rights laws, the effort this year includes approximately 1,000 volunteer monitors, hundreds more than have been previously deployed.

Harris won almost 3 in 4 counties to which monitors were sent. And the remaining 1 in 4, which President Donald Trump won, are usually bluer than their surroundings. In 46 of 49 states for which The Sun has data, the monitors were sent to counties in which Harris performed better than she did in the rest of that state.

This year, monitors’ focus appears to be on cities such as Seattle and Boston, as well as on majority-Black counties such as those containing Montgomery, Alabama, and Memphis, Tennessee — two cities hit by Republican-favored redistricting. The monitored counties are much less white than the rest of the country (45% compared to 64%, respectively) and have substantially higher Black, Hispanic and immigrant populations.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/kRENc/6/The inclusion of all 50 states inevitably targets many historic Republican strongholds. The DOJ will monitor three counties in Kansas and two in Iowa, both states with surprisingly tight Senate races this election year.

Another factor also explains DOJ’s monitoring selections. Eric Neff, the acting chief of the Voting Section within the department’s Civil Rights Division, stated in a court declaration that it had picked the places based on historical practices and, crucially, the locations of U.S. attorneys offices. About three quarters of the counties where monitors were sent in 2026 seem to be home to such an office, a massive increase from the two prior elections.

But even then, the story may not be as simple as it sounds. Regional legal offices tend to be in the sort of urban, educated and diverse cities that typically form Democrats’ base of support.

The expanded program has raised concerns about voter intimidation because of the inclusion of employees from federal law enforcement agencies as well as Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s previous comments that monitors will be tasked with looking for cases of alleged fraud in addition to watching for adherence to voting rights laws.

Election officials in several cities and counties have denied the Justice Department’s request for access to the polls, citing state laws imposing limits on how close feds can get to polling places’ entrances.

Mary Corcoran, the co-founder and executive director of The Save America Movement, said the organization is running a program called Vote Safe that has sent its own poll monitors to Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio and Michigan.

“The Justice Department says it’s watching elections in all 50 states, the largest effort in its history. This isn’t new, but the DOJ’s list is targeted: again and again, Black and Brown communities get extra federal scrutiny,” Corcoran said in a statement. “Those are the same voters Vote Safe was built to stand with, and we’ll be beside them, watching and reporting these poll monitors until the last ballot is cast.”

Another aspect of the Justice Department’s monitoring effort this year is the inclusion of employees from federal law enforcement agencies, such as the Bureau of Prisons. The Justice Department took steps to ensure the monitors aren’t sworn law enforcement officers and instructed monitors not to carry out arrests or bring their guns or insignia, according to filings it submitted to federal court Monday and Tuesday.

entries.title: Federal Judge Blocks Deportation of Afghans to Pakistan and Afghanistan
entries.summary: Attorneys for Afghan immigrants said their clients risk torture and death in their native country.
entries.content:
A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from deporting Afghan nationals to their country or Pakistan.

U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni issued an emergency order Tuesday at the request of attorneys representing Afghan nationals set to be deported to Pakistan and expelled into Afghanistan. They cannot be removed to those countries until at least Sunday.

The order comes a day after Project Rousseau, a New York City nonprofit providing immigrant legal services, sued the Trump administration, claiming the deportations of their Afghan clients were set to take place as early as Tuesday. They said their clients could be in danger if they were sent back to Afghanistan, either directly or via Pakistan.

“Even if the removal from Pakistan to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan does happen, it will be a transfer between two warring parties,” the complaint states. “This creates additional grave risk of persecution, torture, and death.”

Attorneys representing the government told the court Tuesday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not have planned or confirmed deportation flights to send Afghan nationals to Afghanistan or Pakistan this week, according to the order.

More than 150 Afghan immigrants face deportation to Afghanistan via expulsion from Pakistan, including family members of people who helped the U.S. military, The New York Times reported.

The Trump administration has used third-country removals to deport people who have legal protections from returning to countries they fled. In some cases, those deported to countries they’re not from are later expelled to their home countries.

“The consequences could be prison, torture, or worse,” said Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of the refugee advocacy group Global Refuge, following reports of the planned deportations. “For their families, some of whom served alongside U.S. service members, it means losing a loved one, without knowing whether they’ll ever hear from them again.”

entries.title: SCOTUS Weighs Case Over Catholic Preschools That Exclude LGBTQ+ Families
entries.summary: The Trump administration joined arguments against the state of Colorado.
entries.content:
By Lindsay Whitehurst and Michael Kunzelman

The Trump administration joined the Archdiocese of Denver on Tuesday in urging the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling allowing a state-funded preschool program in Colorado to exclude Roman Catholic schools that don't comply with equal-opportunity requirements — the latest religious-rights case before the conservative-majority court.

A win for the Catholic preschools could further narrow a landmark 1990 Supreme Court decision that found religious practices don’t create exemptions from laws that otherwise apply broadly. Written by conservative icon Justice Antonin Scalia in a case over the spiritual use of peyote, a cactus containing mescaline that’s sacred to many Indigenous people, the decision has nevertheless long been a target of the conservative legal movement.

The Denver archdiocese argues that it’s unconstitutional to exclude Catholic preschools from the state's program over their admissions policy for LGBTQ+ families. The Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday on the archdiocese's request to overturn a 10th Circuit decision in the state's favor.

Colorado, meanwhile, says the refusal to admit kids from those families would violate the state’s anti-discrimination law.

But St. Mary Catholic Parish and the Archdiocese of Denver argue that the policy is based on religious teachings about same-sex marriage and that excluding them violates their free-exercise rights.

Nicholas Reaves, an attorney for the archdiocese and two parish preschools, said allowing Catholic schools to participate in Colorado's publicly funded preschools program “will create more seats for everyone, even for families who disagree with Catholic teachings.”

“This is not a zero-sum game," Reaves said. “Letting families use universal preschool funding at Catholic schools won't take away a single seat from the over 2,000 preschools already participating in the program.”

President Donald Trump’s administration is supporting the Catholic institutions. Justice Elena Kagan, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama, said the administration seems to be arguing that children of same-sex marriage can be excluded because “exposing" them to other students "creates a problem.”

"We have a clear line now and you want us to just upend it in one particular area of law," Kagan told Justice Department attorney Sarah Harris.

“No, I think the court currently has a mess,” Harris said.

In the Colorado case, the high court could be sympathetic to the schools. The justices have sided with religious schools in similar disputes before, ruling in recent years that they can’t be excluded from programs in Maine and Montana that provide public aid to private schools. In 2025, though, the court deadlocked over a plan to establish a publicly funded Catholic charter school after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself.

The Colorado universal preschool program was created by a 2020 ballot measure. It provides public funding for preschool at schools chosen by parents.

The plaintiffs, represented by the group Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, say the state has allowed other preschools to prioritize children with disabilities or those from low-income families, so admission based on religious beliefs about gender and same-sex marriage should be allowed, too. The Catholic preschools say their enrollment has dropped 20% since the program started.

Colorado argues that the other admissions decisions are in line with the state’s anti-discrimination rules.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama, asked Reaves if the Catholic school can reject a child simply because their parents are a same-sex couple.

"Is that the bottom line?” she asked.

“If it's the sincere religious exercise of the petitioner, then I think that would be permitted,” Reaves said.

Helen Norton, an attorney for the state, said Colorado is “neutral toward religion” and welcomes religious preschools to participate in the program — provided that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet.

“Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage,” Norton said. “But families have no right to change a school's curriculum.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was nominated to the court by Trump, a Republican, suggested Colorado's law has created an unnecessary “clash of rights” between LGBTQ+ families and "religious believers."

“Just trying to figure out why we're here,” Kavanaugh told Norton. ”Why has this been provoked when there's an ability for everyone to go to the school, a good school that's a fit for them, and respect religious rights?"

Norton said preschools aren't “interchangeable” for parents and children.

“Families are harmed when they're turned away from the publicly funded school that makes their lives work because of the protected class status,” she said.
